items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Why do you put off your homework until the last minute? Ask seven psychologists and you might get seven different answers: your brain chemistry, your habits, your thoughts, your culture, your childhood, your need for growth, even your ancestors. None of them is "the" answer. Each perspective is a lens, and good psychologists switch between them. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Define psychology as a science. Describe the early schools of psychology (background). Explain the seven perspectives: biological, behavioral, cognitive, evolutionary, humanistic, psychodynamic and sociocultural. Compare how different perspectives explain the same behavior, and explain the biopsychosocial model. How this shows up on the exam You won't be asked to recite the history, but you will be asked to apply and compare the seven perspectives: "Which perspective best explains this?" or "How would a cognitive psychologist explain this differently from a behavioral one?" Every unit after this one uses them.

items.x: What psychology is Psychology is the scientific study of behavior (what we do, which can be observed) and mental processes (thoughts, feelings and memories, which have to be inferred). It is built on empiricism : the idea that knowledge should come from careful observation and evidence, not from authority or gut feeling. Background: where it started Psychology became a science in 1879, when Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory in Germany. Early schools included structuralism (Wundt and Titchener, breaking conscious experience into basic elements using introspection , or looking inward and reporting) and functionalism (William James, asking how mental processes help us adapt). Introspection proved too subjective to replicate, which pushed psychology toward more objective methods.

items.x: The seven perspectives Here's one behavior seen through all seven lenses. A student keeps putting off an essay until the night before it's due: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Perspective Focuses on The procrastinating student Biological The brain, neurotransmitters, hormones and genes. Lower activity in the brain's planning areas, and a dopamine "reward" from doing something fun right now. Behavioral Learning from the environment through conditioning and observation; observable behavior. Every time she delays, she's rewarded with relief, so the habit is reinforced. Cognitive Thinking, memory, beliefs and problem-solving. She thinks, "I work best under pressure," and underestimates how long the essay will take. Evolutionary How natural selection shaped behavior that helped our ancestors survive and reproduce. Our ancestors survived by focusing on immediate needs, so we're wired to favor rewards now over rewards later. Humanistic Free will, personal growth and reaching one's potential. She doesn't find the essay meaningful; given more choice, she'd be motivated to grow. Psychodynamic Unconscious motives and conflicts, often from early experience. An unconscious fear of failure, rooted in childhood, makes starting feel threatening. Sociocultural Culture, social norms, family and the people around us. Her friends all leave work to the last minute, and it's seen as normal in her group. Remember all seven B e B rave, C urious, E nergetic, H appy, P atient and S ocial: Biological, Behavioral, Cognitive, Evolutionary, Humanistic, Psychodynamic, Sociocultural. Putting the lenses together Most behavior is too complex for one lens. The biopsychosocial model combines biological , psychological (thoughts, emotions, learning) and sociocultural factors. Most psychologists take an eclectic approach , drawing on several perspectives at once (you'll meet this again in Unit 5).

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do "I knew it all along." "It's obvious." "Everyone knows that." Our intuition is often wrong, and our brains are very good at convincing us that it isn't. The scientific method is psychology's way of checking ideas against evidence instead of against our hunches. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Describe the steps of the scientific method, and tell a theory from a hypothesis. Explain falsifiability and operational definitions. Explain how peer review and replication help science correct itself. Explain confirmation bias, hindsight bias and overconfidence. Explain how cultural norms affect behavior, and the risks of applying psychology in inappropriate or discriminatory ways. How this shows up on the exam On free-response questions you may be asked to state a study's hypothesis and say whether it is falsifiable, or to identify an operational definition and explain how it allows replication. Hindsight bias and overconfidence are classic multiple-choice scenarios.

items.x: The scientific method The scientific method Ask a question → Form a hypothesis → Test it (collect data) → Analyze the results → Draw conclusions → Report, review and replicate Theory A well-tested explanation that organizes many observations and predicts behavior. In science, a theory is not a guess. A theory that sleep helps us process and store memories. Hypothesis A specific, testable prediction , often drawn from a theory. "Students who sleep 8 hours after studying will recall more words than students who sleep 4 hours." Falsifiable A hypothesis is falsifiable if evidence could show it to be wrong. A claim no evidence could ever disprove isn't scientific. Falsifiable: "Exercise reduces anxiety scores." Not falsifiable: "Everything happens for a reason." Operational definition A precise statement of how a variable will be measured in a study, so others can replicate it. "Anxiety" = a score on a 20-question anxiety questionnaire; "sleep" = hours recorded by a sleep tracker. How science checks itself Peer review Before publication, other experts examine a study's methods and conclusions for flaws. A journal sends a study to three psychologists who question how the sample was chosen. Replication Repeating a study, often with different participants or settings, to see if the results hold up. Findings that replicate earn more confidence. A famous finding fails to replicate in ten new labs, so psychologists rethink it.

items.x: Thinking traps and culture Science matters because our everyday thinking has built-in biases: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Bias What it is Example Confirmation bias Looking for, noticing and remembering information that supports what we already believe, while ignoring evidence against it. Believing your favorite team's referee is unfair, and remembering only the calls that went against you. Hindsight bias Believing, after learning an outcome, that we "knew it all along". After the election result, saying, "It was obvious who would win." Overconfidence Being more confident in our judgments and knowledge than the evidence justifies. Being sure you'll finish a project in one evening, and needing three. Culture and the misuse of psychology Cultural norms, expectations and circumstances shape behavior. Making eye contact with a teacher may show respect in one culture and disrespect in another. A finding from one cultural group may not apply to another, so psychologists ask whose behavior a study actually describes. Psychological ideas can also be applied in inappropriate or discriminatory ways : using test scores to label whole groups as less able, or calling a classmate "so OCD" for liking things neat, which trivializes a real disorder. Part of thinking like a psychologist is noticing when an idea is being stretched beyond its evidence.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Every method in psychology is a trade-off. Some describe behavior in rich detail; some reveal relationships across thousands of people; only one can show cause and effect. The skill here is knowing what each method can, and can't, tell you. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Tell experimental and non-experimental methods apart. Describe case studies, correlational studies, naturalistic observation, surveys and meta-analyses, with a strength and a limitation of each. Explain why correlation does not equal causation: the directionality and third variable problems. Tell qualitative and quantitative measures apart, and explain self-report and social desirability bias in surveys. How this shows up on the exam A very common question: "Which research method is this?" followed by "What can the researchers conclude?" If nothing is manipulated and no one is randomly assigned, it is not an experiment, and you can't conclude cause and effect.

items.x: Experimental and non-experimental methods An experiment manipulates an independent variable and uses random assignment to groups (Topic 0.4). Everything else is non-experimental : it can describe and find relationships, but it can't prove cause. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Method What it is Strength Limitation Case study An in-depth study of one person or a small group. Rich detail; useful for rare cases. Results may not generalize to others. Correlational study Measures two or more variables to see whether, and how strongly, they are related. Shows relationships and allows prediction. Can't show cause and effect. Naturalistic observation Watching and recording behavior in its natural setting without interfering. Shows real-life behavior. Can't explain why; people may act differently if they know they're watched. Survey Asking many people questions about their attitudes or behavior. Quick, cheap, large samples. People may not answer accurately or honestly. Meta-analysis A statistical combination of the results of many studies on the same question. A clearer, more reliable overall picture. Only as good as the studies it includes. Being watched changes things When people behave differently because they know they're being observed, it's sometimes called the Hawthorne effect . It's one reason observers try to stay unnoticed.

items.k: Correlation is not causation | Directionality problem | Third variable problem | cause | and | Correlation does not equal causation | illusory correlation
items.x: Correlation is not causation Studies often find that students who use their phones more at night get lower grades. Does phone use cause lower grades? A correlation alone can't tell us, for two reasons: Directionality problem We don't know which variable affects which. Maybe phone use lowers grades, or maybe students who are struggling turn to their phones to escape. A ↔ B: which way does it go? Third variable problem A different, unmeasured variable may cause both. Stress could lead to more phone use and lower grades. C causes both A and B. Correlation does not equal causation If a free-response question describes a correlational study and the conclusion says "causes", "leads to" or "makes", that's your cue to explain the directionality or third variable problem. An illusory correlation is believing two things are related when they aren't, often because a few memorable cases stand out: "Every time I wear these socks, we win."

items.x: Measures and surveys Qualitative measures Collect non-numerical data: words, descriptions, themes. A structured interview asks every participant the same questions in the same order. Interviewing students about how they feel on exam days, then looking for common themes. Quantitative measures Collect numerical data that can be analyzed statistically. A Likert scale asks people to rate their agreement on a scale. "I feel stressed before exams": 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Survey pitfalls Self-report bias People may not report their own behavior accurately because of poor memory or poor self-insight. Students underestimate how many hours a day they spend on their phones. Social desirability bias People answer in ways that make them look good, rather than truthfully. Overreporting how often you recycle or read for pleasure. Wording effects The way a question is worded can change the answers. "Should schools ban phones?" gets different answers from "Should students be allowed to keep phones for emergencies?"

items.x: Placebos and blind procedures Placebo An inactive substance or fake treatment that looks like the real one, given to the control group. A sugar pill that looks exactly like the caffeine pill. Placebo effect Changes in behavior or health caused by expecting a treatment to work, not by the treatment itself. Procedure Who doesn't know which group is which? What it controls Single-blind The participants . items.x: Populations and samples Population The whole group a researcher wants to draw conclusions about. All secondary school students in the UAE. Sample The subset of the population who actually take part. The 600 students who complete the survey. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Sampling method How participants are chosen Effect on the results Random sampling Every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen. Most likely to give a representative sample , so results can be generalized. Stratified sampling The population is divided into subgroups (such as grade levels or emirates), and people are randomly sampled from each in proportion. Makes sure key subgroups are represented. Convenience sampling Choosing people who are easy to reach . Quick and cheap, but the sample is often unrepresentative. A representative sample closely matches the population on important characteristics (age, background, school type). When it doesn't, the study has sampling bias , which limits generalizability : how far the results can be applied to the wider population. Volunteer bias is one source: people who choose to take part may differ from those who don't.

items.k: Why representation matters | appropriately represented | don't | A sample size trap
items.x: Why representation matters For much of psychology's history, many studies were run on university students from a narrow range of countries. Their findings were then treated as if they described all people. When participants are appropriately represented (different ages, cultures, backgrounds and abilities), results are more accurate and fair, and we find out where findings don't apply. A sample size trap A big sample isn't automatically a good one. A million people surveyed through one social media app still only represents that app's users. How participants are chosen matters more than how many there are.

items.x: The normal curve and skew Many traits, such as height or intelligence test scores, fall in a normal curve : a symmetrical, bell-shaped distribution where the mean, median and mode are the same and most scores sit near the middle. Percentile rank is the percentage of scores at or below a given score. Scoring in the 84th percentile means you scored as well as or better than 84% of test-takers (about 1 SD above the mean on a normal curve). Skewed distributions Positive skew The tail points to the right (toward high scores). Most scores are low; a few very high scores pull the mean above the median . Scores on a very hard test: most students score low, a few score very high. Negative skew The tail points to the left (toward low scores). Most scores are high; a few very low scores pull the mean below the median . Scores on a very easy test: most students score high, a few score very low. A bimodal distribution has two peaks , which often means two different groups are mixed together: for example, test scores from students who did and didn't attend a review session. Follow the tail The skew is named after the direction the tail points, not where the hump is. And the mean always gets dragged toward the tail.

More hours of revision, higher exam scores. Negative correlation The variables move in opposite directions . More hours on social media at night, fewer hours of sleep. Regression toward the mean Regression toward the mean is the tendency for extreme scores to be followed by scores closer to the average as more data are collected. A player who has an amazing game is likely to have a more ordinary one next; a student who does unusually badly on one quiz will probably do better on the next, with or without any intervention.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Some of psychology's most famous studies would never be allowed today. Participants were deceived, frightened or harmed, sometimes with no idea what they had signed up for. Modern research ethics exist so that people (and animals) who help science aren't hurt by it. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain the role of institutional review for research with humans and non-human animals. Explain informed consent and informed assent. Explain protection from harm, confidentiality and anonymity. Explain when deception and confederates may be used, and the purpose of debriefing. Were minors' parents asked? Were participants debriefed? Was their data kept private?

items.x: Ethical guidelines Psychologists follow ethical guidelines from organizations such as the American Psychological Association (APA) . Before a study begins, it must be approved by a review board: Institutional review board (IRB) Reviews research with human participants before it starts, checking that risks are minimized and justified by the benefits. A university IRB asks a researcher to remove a stressful task from a study with teenagers. Animal care committee (IACUC) Reviews research with non-human animals , making sure animals are cared for humanely and suffering is minimized. A committee checks the housing and treatment of lab rats in a learning study. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Guideline What it requires Example Informed consent Participants are told what the study involves, including risks, and agree to take part. They know they can withdraw at any time . Before a stress study, adult participants read and sign a form describing the tasks. Informed assent Participants who can't give legal consent (such as children under 18) agree to take part, and a parent or guardian gives consent. A 15-year-old agrees to a memory study, and her parents sign the consent form. Protection from harm Researchers minimize physical and psychological risks, and stop or help if harm occurs. Participants who become upset during a task are offered support and the chance to stop. Confidentiality Participants' information is kept private ; only the researchers can link data to names. Names are stored separately and never published. Anonymity No identifying information is ever collected , so data can't be linked to any person. An online survey that never asks for names or emails. Deception Misleading participants about the study's true purpose. Allowed only if necessary, if the risk is low, and if participants are debriefed. It may involve confederates : people working with the researcher who pretend to be participants. Participants are told a study is about vision, when it's really about conformity, and a confederate gives wrong answers on purpose. Debriefing After the study, participants are told its true purpose , any deception is explained, and questions are answered. At the end of the conformity study, the researcher explains the confederate's role.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Why are you the way you are? Your genes had a say. So did your family, your friends, your school and the place you grew up. This topic is about how psychologists think about those two sets of influences, and how they try to separate them. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain heredity (nature) and environment (nurture), and why psychologists say they interact rather than compete. Explain the evolutionary perspective and natural selection, and why eugenics is a misuse of those ideas. Explain what twin studies, family studies and adoption studies can (and cannot) tell us about genes and behavior. How this shows up on the exam Expect a short study description followed by "Which research design is this?" or "What does this finding suggest?" Your job is to spot the design (twin, family or adoption) and explain the logic: who shares genes, who shares an environment, and what a similarity or difference between them points to. Not on the exam Detailed genetics: genotype, phenotype, DNA, chromosomes, and dominant or recessive genes. You only need the psychology of heredity, not the biology class version.

items.k: Nature and nurture | Heredity ("nature") | Environment ("nurture") | Not "versus", but "and" | nature versus nurture | Epigenetics
items.x: Nature and nurture Heredity ("nature") The genetic or predisposed characteristics you inherit, which influence your physical traits, behavior and mental processes. What you were born with. Environment ("nurture") The external factors you experience: family interactions, education, friends, culture, the places you live. What happens to you after that. Not "versus", but "and" The old framing was nature versus nurture , as if one side had to win. Psychologists now treat it as nature and nurture : the two interact to shape almost everything about us. Here's the thing. Asking which one matters more is a bit like asking whether a photo's quality comes from the camera or from the light. Change either one and the picture changes. Height is strongly influenced by genes, yet a child who is poorly fed will not reach the height their genes allowed. A teenager may inherit a quick musical ear, but without lessons, practice and a reason to play, that ear never becomes a skill. Going further (useful, but not named in the CED) Epigenetics shows how deep the interaction goes. Your environment and experiences can influence which genes are switched on or off, without changing the DNA itself. It is one reason identical twins can grow less alike over a lifetime.

items.x: The evolutionary perspective The evolutionary perspective asks: how might this behavior have helped our ancestors survive and reproduce? It draws on Charles Darwin's idea of natural selection . Traits that helped individuals survive and have children were more likely to be passed on; traits that did not tended to fade out over many generations. Psychologists use this lens to explain tendencies that show up across cultures: We tend to love sweet and fatty foods, which were rare and valuable sources of energy for our ancestors. We learn to fear snakes, heights and spiders far more quickly than we learn to fear cars or electrical sockets, even though modern dangers are often deadlier. Notice the word tendencies . The evolutionary perspective explains why some behaviors come easily to humans. It does not mean those behaviors are fixed, right or unchangeable. Eugenics: a misuse of evolutionary ideas Eugenics was the belief that a population could be "improved" by encouraging some people to have children and preventing others. In the twentieth century it was used to justify forced sterilization and discrimination against groups labeled "unfit". The CED includes it as a warning: scientific ideas about heredity have been twisted to discriminate against people, and psychology has a responsibility not to repeat that. Keep these apart Natural selection describes how traits spread over generations. Eugenics was a human policy that tried to control who could reproduce. If a question describes a government or group deciding whose children are "desirable", the answer is eugenics.

items.x: How researchers separate genes from environment You cannot ethically assign children to different families just to see what happens. So researchers use situations that already exist and compare people who share different amounts of genes and environment. Twin studies Compare identical twins (who share virtually all their genes) with fraternal twins (who share about half, like ordinary siblings). If identical twins are more alike on a trait, genes probably play a role. The strongest version: identical twins raised apart. Family studies Check whether a trait runs in families, and whether closer relatives are more alike than distant ones. Weakness: families share homes as well as genes. Adoption studies Compare adopted children with their biological parents (shared genes) and their adoptive parents (shared environment). Which family do they end up resembling? Reading the evidence Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. If researchers find that... It points toward... Identical twins are more alike on a trait than fraternal twins A genetic contribution to the trait Identical twins raised in different homes are still very alike A genetic contribution, since their environments differed Adopted children resemble their biological parents more than their adoptive parents A genetic contribution Adopted children resemble their adoptive parents more than their biological parents An environmental contribution A trait runs in families Genes or shared environment, or both; a family study alone cannot tell them apart Two long-running examples you may see named: the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart , which tracked identical twins separated early in life, and the Colorado Adoption Project , which followed adopted children alongside both sets of parents for decades. Classic trap: "proves it is genetic" These studies estimate how much genes contribute to differences between people. They never show that a trait is purely genetic, and they cannot tell you how much of one particular person's personality came from their genes.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Think about the minutes before a big exam. Nobody tells your heart to race or your mouth to go dry, yet both happen. Meanwhile you are choosing, on purpose, to pick up a pen. Two very different jobs, both handled by your nervous system. This topic is the map of how that system is organized. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Tell the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) apart, and say what belongs to each. Explain the difference between the somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (involuntary) nervous systems. Predict what the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions do to the body in a given situation. How this shows up on the exam You will usually get a person in a situation (a scare, a race, a calm evening) and be asked which division of the nervous system is most active. The most common mistake is swapping what the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions do to heart rate, pupils and digestion, so learn that table cold.

items.x: The map of the nervous system Tap any box to see what it does. Each split answers one question: is it in the brain and spinal cord or not? Is it voluntary or not? Is it speeding you up or calming you down? Tap a box in the diagram, or use the buttons. Nervous system CNS PNS Somatic Autonomic Sympathetic Parasympathetic The nervous system Your body's communication network. It splits into two big parts: the central nervous system, which makes decisions, and the peripheral nervous system, which carries messages between the central system and the rest of your body. Central nervous system (CNS) The brain and spinal cord . It takes in information, processes it and sends out instructions, and it interacts with every process in the body. If it is inside your skull or spine, it is CNS. Brain The main control center for thinking, feeling, memory and voluntary movement. Topic 1.4 takes you through its parts. Spinal cord The information highway between the brain and the body. It also handles simple reflexes on its own, like pulling your hand from something hot (the reflex arc in Topic 1.3). The spinal cord is part of the CNS , not the PNS. Peripheral nervous system (PNS) All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. It relays messages from the CNS out to the muscles and organs, and brings information from the body back in. It has two branches: somatic and autonomic . Somatic nervous system Controls voluntary movement of your skeletal muscles: raising your hand, typing an answer, kicking a ball. It also carries sensory information from your skin and muscles back to the CNS. Hook: Somatic = skeletal muscles, by choice. Autonomic nervous system Controls involuntary processes that keep you alive without you thinking about them: heartbeat, breathing, digestion, sweating. It has two divisions that work in opposite directions: sympathetic and parasympathetic . Hook: Autonomic = automatic. Sympathetic division Arouses the body for action when you face a threat, a challenge or stress: the fight-or-flight response. Heart rate and breathing speed up, pupils widen, digestion slows down, and stored energy is released. It works alongside the hormone adrenaline (Topic 1.3). Hook: Sympathetic = sprint. Parasympathetic division Calms the body once the challenge has passed and helps it conserve energy: rest and digest. Heart rate and breathing slow down, pupils narrow, and digestion starts up again. Hook: Parasympathetic = pause.

items.x: Sympathetic versus parasympathetic Picture Fatima on the morning of her AP exam. As she walks into the hall, her heart is pounding, her breathing is quick, her mouth is dry and her stomach feels like it has stopped working. That is her sympathetic division at work. Two hours later, the exam is over, she sits down with her friends and a snack, and everything slows down again. That is the parasympathetic division taking over. items.x: Two kinds of cells Neurons: the messengers Neurons carry information. Inside the cell the message is electrical; between cells it becomes chemical. Every behavior and mental process you will study in this course is built on neurons talking to each other. Glial cells: the support crew Glial cells keep neurons working. They give structure, insulate (for example, the myelin around many axons), support communication and clear away waste. The neuron is the cell that carries the message itself. The reflex arc: your spinal cord acts first You grab the handle of a car door that has been sitting in the afternoon sun. Before you have even thought "hot", your hand has already let go. That is a reflex arc, and it needs three types of neurons: 1 · In Sensory neuron Carries the "this is burning" signal from your skin to the spinal cord. 2 · Middle Interneuron Sits inside the spinal cord (part of the central nervous system) and passes the signal straight across, while also sending it up to the brain. 3 · Out Motor neuron Carries the command to your hand muscles: let go. The pain arrives a moment later, once your brain catches up. Move first, feel second: that order is what makes reflexes protective. It is also a nice example of the central and peripheral nervous systems (Topic 1.2) working together. Memory hook S-I-M : S ensory brings it in, the I nterneuron sits in the middle, the M otor neuron sends it out to the muscles.

items.x: How a neuron fires Neural firing happens in the same orderly sequence every time. Step through it below and watch where you are on the graph of the neuron's charge. Step 1 of 7 Resting potential: charged and ready At rest, the inside of the neuron is slightly negative compared with the outside (about -70 millivolts). Resting does not mean switched off. The neuron is charged and ready to go, like a phone on standby. Step 2 of 7 Messages arrive and add up Other neurons send signals to this neuron's dendrites. Excitatory messages nudge the charge up toward firing. Inhibitory messages push it down, away from firing. The neuron is constantly adding these up. Step 3 of 7 Threshold: fire or don't If the total reaches the threshold (about -55 millivolts), the neuron fires. If it falls short, nothing happens. This is the all-or-none principle : a neuron never fires halfway, and a stronger push does not make a bigger impulse. Step 4 of 7 Depolarization: the action potential Positively charged ions rush into the cell, and the charge flips from negative to positive. This electrical impulse, the action potential , travels down the axon toward the terminal. Myelin, the insulation made by glial cells, helps it travel faster. Step 5 of 7 Refractory period: recharging Right after firing, the neuron resets back to its resting charge. During this short refractory period it cannot fire again, a bit like a camera flash that needs a second to recharge before the next photo. Step 6 of 7 The message turns chemical At the axon terminal, the electrical signal triggers the release of neurotransmitters into the synapse , the tiny gap between two neurons. They cross the gap and lock onto receptor sites on the receiving neuron, sending it an excitatory or inhibitory message (back to Step 2 for the next neuron). Step 7 of 7 Cleanup: reuptake Leftover neurotransmitters do not hang around in the gap. Some are broken down, and many are pulled back into the sending neuron to be reused. That recycling is called reuptake . Keep it in mind: several drugs work by interfering with exactly this step. Back Next step Classic trap: "a stronger stimulus makes a bigger spike" A harder pinch does not make each action potential bigger. Every action potential is the same size. Your brain reads intensity from how often neurons fire and how many fire at once. Think of a doorbell, not a volume knob: an urgent visitor rings more often, not louder.

items.x: How psychoactive drugs change the message Psychoactive drugs change behavior and mental processes by interfering with neural communication. The CED names specific drugs as examples, so the exam uses them. What you are learning here is what each one does to neural activity. Three ways a drug can act Think of a neurotransmitter as a key and a receptor site as a lock. Agonist Mimics or boosts a neurotransmitter, so its effect gets stronger. Opioids, for example, act like endorphins at their receptors. A copied key that also opens the lock. Antagonist Blocks the receptor, so the real neurotransmitter cannot deliver its message. A drug that blocks acetylcholine receptors at the muscles would cause weakness. Gum stuck in the keyhole. Reuptake inhibitor Stops the sending neuron from pulling the neurotransmitter back (Step 7), so more stays in the synapse for longer. SSRI antidepressants do this with serotonin; cocaine does it with dopamine. Someone blocking the recycling bin. Four drug categories Category CED examples Effect on neural activity What you might observe Stimulants Caffeine, cocaine Increase neural activity More alert and energetic; can bring restlessness, anxiety and trouble sleeping. Depressants Alcohol Decrease neural activity Slower reactions, poorer judgment and memory, drowsiness. Hallucinogens Marijuana Distort perception and/or thinking Changes in how things look, sound or feel; altered sense of time. Opioids Heroin Relieve pain Pain relief and drowsiness; a very high risk of addiction. Tolerance, addiction and withdrawal These three describe how repeated drug use changes the brain over time, and they usually come as a chain: Tolerance: the brain adapts to the drug, so the same dose has less effect and more is needed to feel the same thing. Addiction: compulsive use that continues despite harm to the person's health, relationships or responsibilities. Withdrawal: the unpleasant (sometimes dangerous) physical and psychological symptoms that appear when a person with an addiction stops using the drug.

items.x: Check yourself Answer each one in your head (or out loud) before you open it. 1. Rania touches a scorching car door handle and lets go before she feels any pain. Which neuron passes the signal across inside her spinal cord? The interneuron. The sensory neuron brings the signal in, the interneuron in the spinal cord passes it straight to the motor neuron, and the motor neuron tells her hand to let go. The brain hears about it a moment later. 2. Yousef stubs his toe hard, and it hurts far more than a light bump. Did his neurons fire bigger action potentials? No. By the all-or-none principle, every action potential is the same size. The harder knock made more neurons fire, and fire more often, and that is what his brain read as "this really hurts". 3. A medication stops the sending neuron from reabsorbing serotonin. What kind of drug action is this, and what happens in the synapse? A reuptake inhibitor. More serotonin stays in the synapse for longer, so its message keeps being received. This is how SSRI antidepressants are designed to work. 4. A toxin blocks the acetylcholine receptors on muscle cells. Agonist or antagonist? Predict what the person would experience. An antagonist. Acetylcholine can no longer deliver its message to the muscles, so you would expect muscle weakness or, at high doses, paralysis. Notice that this looks a lot like myasthenia gravis, where the receptors are blocked by the immune system instead. 5. Mariam skipped breakfast. By 11 a.m. her stomach is growling and she cannot focus in class. Which hormone is rising? Ghrelin. It is released when the stomach is empty and increases hunger. After lunch, leptin and a full stomach help switch the hunger signal off. 6. A drug strengthens the effect of GABA. Would you expect the person to become calmer or more alert? Calmer. GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, so a GABA agonist makes firing less likely: slower reactions, relaxation, drowsiness. This is the same direction as depressants such as alcohol, which boost GABA's effect. items.x: The lobes of the cortex, and what lies below The cerebral cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, split into two hemispheres and four lobes on each side. Tap any part of the diagram to see what it does. Left hemisphere seen from the side. A simplified sketch, not to scale. Frontal lobe Prefrontal cortex Motor cortex Broca's area Parietal lobe Somatosensory cortex Temporal lobe Wernicke's area Occipital lobe Cerebellum Brain stem Frontal lobes Just behind your forehead. They handle higher-order thinking , executive functioning (planning, decision-making, self-control) and language processing . They contain the prefrontal cortex, the motor cortex and Broca's area. Case study link: after an iron rod passed through Phineas Gage's frontal lobe in 1848, he survived, but people who knew him said his personality and self-control changed dramatically. Prefrontal cortex The very front part of the frontal lobes. It is the center of executive functioning : planning ahead, weighing consequences, controlling impulses, making judgments. It is one of the last brain areas to finish maturing, continuing into the mid-twenties. Motor cortex A strip at the rear of the frontal lobes that controls most voluntary skeletal movement. It sends commands out , so stimulating it makes a body part move . It works contralaterally: the left motor cortex moves the right side of the body. Broca's area Usually in the left frontal lobe . Responsible for speech production . Damage causes a type of aphasia in which the person mostly understands language but speaks slowly, with great effort, in broken phrases. Parietal lobes Near the back of the crown of your head. They contain the somatosensory cortex (touch) and association areas that process and organize information, for example combining what you see and feel to judge where things are in space. Somatosensory cortex A strip at the front of the parietal lobes , right behind the motor cortex. It processes touch sensitivity : pressure, temperature, pain. It takes information in , so stimulating it makes a person feel a touch. Sensitive areas like the lips and fingertips get the most cortex. Temporal lobes On the sides of the brain, near your ears (think "temples"). They handle auditory processing (hearing) and linguistic processing, including understanding speech in Wernicke's area. The hippocampus sits on the inside of each temporal lobe. Wernicke's area Usually in the left temporal lobe . Responsible for speech comprehension . Damage causes a type of aphasia in which speech flows easily but makes little sense, and the person struggles to understand others. Occipital lobes At the back of the brain. They process visual information . Damage here can cause visual problems even when the eyes are healthy, including face blindness and blindsight (Topic 1.6). Cerebellum The "little brain" at the back, below the occipital lobes. It coordinates muscle movement , maintains balance and supports some procedural learning , like riding a bike or touch-typing. Alcohol disrupts it, which is one reason a drunk person struggles to walk in a straight line. Brain stem Where the brain meets the spinal cord. It controls basic life functions . Its lowest part, the medulla , regulates breathing and heart rate. The reticular activating system runs through it too (see the table below). Serious damage here is often fatal. Memory hooks Occipital sounds like "optical": vision at the back. Temporal sits by your temples and ears: hearing. Parietal on top: "pat" the top of your head to feel touch. Frontal at the front: plans what you do next. And the motor and sensory strips sit side by side: motor in front, sensation behind .

items.x: Two hemispheres, one brain Contralateral organization Each hemisphere mainly controls and senses the opposite side of the body. A stroke in the left hemisphere usually affects movement on the right side of the body. Vision works the same way by visual field: what you see on your right side is processed by your left hemisphere. Split-brain research For some people with severe epilepsy, surgeons cut the corpus callosum to stop seizures spreading from one side of the brain to the other. Afterwards, the two hemispheres can no longer share information directly, which let researchers test what each side does on its own. A split-brain patient is shown a word... It goes to... What happens In the right visual field The left hemisphere They can say the word out loud, because language is usually in the left hemisphere. In the left visual field The right hemisphere They usually cannot say it, but their left hand (controlled by the right hemisphere) can pick out the matching object. Findings like these show that the hemispheres may specialize . Language areas (Broca's and Wernicke's) are typically in the left hemisphere, while the right tends to contribute more to tasks like recognizing faces and reading spatial layouts. Classic trap: "left-brained and right-brained people" Specialization does not mean some people are logical "left-brainers" and others creative "right-brainers". In a healthy brain the hemispheres constantly work together through the corpus callosum. That popular idea is a myth. Brain plasticity Plasticity is the brain's ability to rewire itself, change existing connections and create new ones throughout life. It allows other areas to take over some of the work of a damaged area, which is why stroke patients can regain abilities with therapy. Plasticity is strongest in childhood: children who have had an entire hemisphere removed to stop severe seizures can recover a surprising amount of function.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do You will spend roughly a third of your life asleep. That is not wasted time: your brain is busy all night, cycling through stages that look nothing alike. This topic covers what happens across a night, why we sleep and dream, and what happens when sleep goes wrong. (It also explains why the night before an exam is the worst time to give up sleep.) By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain consciousness, the circadian rhythm, and how jet lag and shift work disrupt it. Identify the five sleep disorders in the CED from a description. How this shows up on the exam Expect EEG descriptions ("fast, irregular waves, but the muscles are completely relaxed") and sleep scenarios ("a child walks to the kitchen at midnight and remembers nothing"). The most common errors: placing sleepwalking in REM (it happens in deep NREM sleep), and forgetting that REM, not Stage 3, is the stage linked with dreaming. items.x: Consciousness and your body clock Consciousness is your awareness of your thoughts, feelings, behavior and what is happening inside and around you. It is not simply on or off: it has levels. Sleep and wakefulness are two different types of consciousness. Even asleep, your brain still notices some things, which is why you can sleep through traffic but wake up when someone says your name. The circadian rhythm Your sleep/wake cycle follows a circadian rhythm , an internal body clock that runs on roughly a 24-hour cycle. Light is its main signal: as it gets dark, the hormone melatonin rises (Topic 1.3) and you start to feel sleepy. Jet lag Fly from Dubai to New York and your body clock still thinks it is Dubai time. You are wide awake at 3 a.m. and exhausted at lunch, until your rhythm catches up with the new time zone. Shift work Nurses, pilots and security staff who work through the night ask their bodies to be awake when the circadian rhythm says sleep. Over time this can harm alertness, mood and health.

items.k: A night of sleep, stage by stage | Awake | Stage 1 (NREM): drifting off | Stage 2 (NREM): true sleep | Stage 3 (NREM): deep sleep | REM sleep: paradoxical sleep | EEG patterns | Alert | Relaxed, eyes closed | Stage 1 | hypnagogic sensations | Stage 2 | sleep spindles | K-complexes | Stage 3 | REM | paradoxical | dreaming | REM rebound | Two patterns to remember | Deep sleep early, dreams late
items.x: A night of sleep, stage by stage Researchers tell the stages of sleep apart by their EEG patterns , the shape of the brain waves recorded from the scalp. You move through a full cycle of stages about every 90 minutes, four to six times a night. Tap a stage to see its brain waves and what is going on. Awake Stage 1 Stage 2 Stage 3 REM Awake Alert fast, small waves (beta) Relaxed, eyes closed slower, regular waves (alpha) When you are alert and thinking, brain waves are fast and small. As you relax and get drowsy, they slow into a more regular rhythm. Stage 1 (NREM): drifting off Stage 1 slower, irregular waves (theta) A short, light transition into sleep, lasting only a few minutes. You are easy to wake and may insist you were not asleep at all. As you enter it, you may have hypnagogic sensations : the feeling of falling, a sudden jerk, or brief dream-like images. Stage 2 (NREM): true sleep Stage 2 sleep spindles and K-complexes Now you are clearly asleep and harder to wake. The EEG shows sleep spindles (short bursts of fast activity) and K-complexes (single large waves). You spend more of the night in Stage 2 than in any other stage. Stage 3 (NREM): deep sleep Stage 3 slow, large waves (delta) The deepest sleep, with slow, large delta waves. You are very hard to wake, and if someone does wake you, you feel groggy and confused. Look at the graph: Stage 3 is long early in the night and almost disappears by morning, because NREM stages get shorter as the night goes on . Sleepwalking and sleep talking happen here. REM sleep: paradoxical sleep REM fast waves, almost like being awake Your eyes dart around under your eyelids (Rapid Eye Movement). It is called paradoxical sleep because the brain waves look almost like being awake, yet the body is at its most relaxed: your major muscles are effectively paralyzed. This is when most dreaming happens. Notice on the graph that REM periods get longer as the night goes on , so the last hours of sleep are full of dreams. If you are deprived of REM sleep (say, after several short nights), you will enter REM faster and spend more time in it when you finally sleep properly. This is REM rebound . Two patterns to remember Deep sleep early, dreams late. Stage 3 shrinks across the night while REM periods grow. Cutting your sleep short in the morning mostly costs you REM.

items.s: Why do we sleep? Why do we dream?
items.k: Why do we sleep? Why do we dream? | Why we sleep | Restoration theory | Memory consolidation theory | Why we dream | Activation-synthesis theory | Consolidation theory of dreams | Apply it to yourself
items.x: Why do we sleep? Why do we dream? These are two separate questions, and the CED gives you two theories for each. Keep them in separate boxes in your head. Why we sleep Restoration theory Sleep restores the body and brain, replenishing resources used up during the day and repairing tissue. Sleep as overnight charging. Memory consolidation theory Sleep helps the brain organize and strengthen (consolidate) the memories formed during the day. Sleep as saving your work. Why we dream Activation-synthesis theory During REM sleep the brain stem fires off random neural activity. The cortex tries to make sense of it by weaving it into a story: the dream. Dreams as the brain's best guess. Consolidation theory of dreams Dreams are part of how the brain sorts, processes and stores the day's experiences and memories. Dreams as the brain filing. Apply it to yourself Pulling an all-nighter before a test works against both "why we sleep" theories: your brain has had no time to restore itself, and no chance to consolidate what you studied. The research on sleep and memory is one of the strongest arguments for going to bed.

items.x: Sleep disorders: the five you need Sleep problems affect physical and cognitive performance during the day: attention, memory, mood and reaction time. Treating sleep disorders and keeping a regular sleep schedule can improve both daytime performance and overall well-being. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Disorder What happens Clue to spot it Insomnia Ongoing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep. Lies awake for hours; wakes repeatedly; tired all day. Narcolepsy Sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep during the day, sometimes dropping straight into REM. Falls asleep mid-conversation or mid-task without warning. REM sleep behavior disorder The normal muscle paralysis of REM is missing, so the person acts out their dreams. Kicks, punches or shouts while dreaming; may injure themselves or a family member. Sleep apnea Breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, briefly waking the person (often without them knowing). Loud snoring and gasping; exhausted despite a "full" night in bed. Somnambulism (sleepwalking) Walking or doing other actions while still asleep, during deep NREM (Stage 3) sleep. Usually early in the night; no memory of it the next day; more common in children.

items.x: From the world to the brain Sensation is the process of detecting information from the environment and transducing it, which means converting it into neural messages the brain can process. What the brain then does with those messages (recognizing, organizing, interpreting) is perception , which you will meet in Unit 2. Concept What it means Everyday example Absolute threshold The weakest stimulus you can detect at least 50 percent of the time . The faintest phone vibration you notice about half the time it buzzes. Just-noticeable difference (difference threshold) The smallest change in a stimulus you can detect at least half the time. How much sugar has to be added to your karak before you notice it is sweeter. Weber's law The just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount. Adding one candle to two is obvious; adding one to fifty is not. Sensory adaptation Sensitivity drops when a stimulus stays the same, so you stop noticing it. You walk into a majlis full of oud perfume and stop smelling it after a few minutes. Sensory interaction The senses constantly work together and influence each other. Food tastes flat when your nose is blocked. Synesthesia Stimulation of one sense is also experienced through another. A person who sees particular colors whenever they hear certain musical notes. Try it: Weber's law and your school bag For lifted weight, the just-noticeable difference is roughly 2 percent of the starting weight. Move the slider to change how heavy your bag already is. Starting weight of your bag: The heavier the bag, the bigger the change needs to be. That is Weber's law: the change you notice depends on the proportion , not the amount. (Other senses have their own percentages; 2 percent is an approximate figure used for illustration.)

items.x: Vision Getting light onto the retina Light enters the eye and the lens focuses it onto the retina , the light-sensitive surface at the back of the eye. The lens changes shape to focus on near or far objects, a process called accommodation . When the focusing goes wrong: Nearsightedness: the image focuses in front of the retina, so distant objects look blurry (you can see near things clearly). Farsightedness: the image focuses behind the retina, so nearby objects look blurry (you can see far things clearly). Rods and cones Cells in the retina capture visual information and transduce it into neural messages. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Rods Cones Where The periphery (edges) of the retina Concentrated in the fovea, the center of the retina Detect Shapes and movement, but not color Color and fine detail Work best in Low light Bright light Also Play a big part in adjusting to the dark (dark adaptation) Come in three types: blue (short wavelengths), green (medium) and red (long) Memory hook C ones see C olor in the C enter. Rods take over in the dark, which is why everything looks gray on a night-time walk. The blind spot Where the visual (optic) nerve leaves the eye there are no receptor cells, so each eye has a blind spot . You never notice it, because your brain fills in the gap to give you a complete-looking picture. That is evidence the retina sends the brain an incomplete image. Try it: find your blind spot Close your left eye. With your right eye, stare at the + . Slowly move your face toward and away from the screen. At one distance the dot will vanish. + Seeing color: two theories, both right Color vision is explained by both theories. They describe different stages of processing. Trichromatic theory The retina has three types of cones, most sensitive to blue, green and red light. Every color you see comes from the combination of signals from those three. Three cones, mixing like a screen's pixels. Opponent-process theory Further along, ganglion cells in the retina work in opposing pairs: red/green, blue/yellow and black/white . When one side of a pair is activated, the other is not. This explains afterimages . Three pairs, each a tug of war. Try it: an afterimage Press start and stare at the small orange dot in the middle for 20 seconds without moving your eyes. The picture will then disappear. Start You should see the opposite colors: a reddish circle where the green was, a bluish square where the yellow was, and a lighter bar where the black was. The cells you tired out stopped firing, so their opponents took over for a moment. When vision goes wrong Color vision deficiency: damage or irregularities in one or more types of cone or ganglion cell (most often red/green, sometimes blue/yellow). Dichromatism means seeing with only two working cone types; monochromatism means seeing no color at all, only shades of light and dark. Prosopagnosia (face blindness): the person can see faces perfectly well but cannot recognize them, even a family member's. Blindsight: the person says they cannot see objects in part of their visual field, yet can still respond to them, for example pointing to where something is or stepping around it. Both prosopagnosia and blindsight come from damage to the parts of the brain responsible for vision (mainly the occipital lobes, Topic 1.4), not from damage to the eyes.

Three theories | Where is that sound coming from? | Two kinds of hearing loss | Conduction deafness | Sensorineural deafness | Wavelength | pitch | Amplitude | loudness | places | same rate | groups | Memory hook | Place | where | Frequency | how fast | Volley | taking turns | Sound localization | conduct | hair cells | auditory nerve | Spot the difference | Conduction | Sensorineural | sensory receptors or nerve
items.x: Hearing Sound is the movement of air molecules in waves. Two features of a sound wave matter here: Wavelength determines pitch . Short wavelengths (high frequency) sound high, like a whistle. Long wavelengths (low frequency) sound low, like a bass drum. Amplitude (the height of the wave) determines loudness . How do we hear pitch? Three theories Theory The idea Explains best Place theory Different places along the basilar membrane in the cochlea vibrate most for different pitches. The brain reads pitch from where the hair cells are being stimulated. High pitches Frequency theory The auditory nerve fires at the same rate as the sound wave's frequency. The brain reads pitch from how fast the nerve fires. Low pitches Volley theory A single neuron cannot fire fast enough for mid-range pitches, so groups of neurons take turns firing, like a team of archers sending volleys of arrows. Together they match the frequency. Middle pitches, beyond what one neuron can manage Memory hook Place = where on the membrane. Frequency = how fast the nerve fires. Volley = taking turns to go faster than one neuron can. Where is that sound coming from? Sound localization is how we work out where a sound comes from. A sound on your right reaches your right ear slightly sooner and slightly louder than your left. Your brain uses those tiny differences in timing and loudness to place the sound. Sounds directly in front of you or behind you are the hardest to place, because they reach both ears at the same moment. Two kinds of hearing loss Conduction deafness Damage to the mechanical parts that conduct sound to the inner ear, such as the eardrum or the tiny bones of the middle ear. Sound simply does not get through well. Hearing aids that amplify sound often help. Sensorineural deafness Damage to the hair cells in the cochlea or to the auditory nerve , often from aging or long exposure to loud noise. Sound arrives, but it is not turned into neural messages properly. Cochlear implants can help some people. Spot the difference Conduction = the sound can't get in . Sensorineural = the sound gets in, but the sensory receptors or nerve can't pass it on. A teenager who plays music through earphones at full volume every day is risking sensorineural loss.

items.x: The chemical senses: smell and taste Smell (olfaction) Receptors in the nose detect odor molecules and transduce them into neural messages. Smell is special in one way you need to know: it is the only sense not processed first in the thalamus . Smell signals travel more directly to brain areas linked with emotion and memory, which may be why a scent can bring back a memory so vividly. Pheromones are chemical messages, detected through the olfactory system, that animals of the same species use to signal to one another. Taste (gustation) Receptors on the tongue and in the mouth detect six basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami (savory, like a rich broth) and oleogustus (the taste of fat). The number of taste receptors a person has affects how strongly they taste: Supertasters have the most receptors and taste things intensely, especially bitter flavors like strong coffee or dark green vegetables. Medium tasters are in between. Nontasters have the fewest receptors and find flavors milder. Smell and taste work together What you call "taste" is mostly the two chemical senses interacting. Without smell, taste is muted or missing, which is why food seems flavorless when you have a blocked nose. This is a clear example of sensory interaction .

items.x: Touch, pain, balance and movement Touch Receptors in the skin detect pressure, warmth, cold and pain, and the brain processes them (in the somatosensory cortex, Topic 1.4). One surprise the CED wants you to know: the sensation of "hot" is produced when warm and cold receptors are activated at the same time . Pain Pain is processed both in the body and in the brain, which is why the same injury can hurt more or less depending on what you are paying attention to. Gate control theory proposes a neural "gate" in the spinal cord that can open to let pain signals through to the brain or close to block them. Rubbing a bumped elbow, or being absorbed in a match, can help close the gate. Phantom limb sensation is when people who have lost a limb still feel sensations or pain where the limb used to be. It shows that pain can be produced by the brain even when the body part is gone. Balance and body movement Vestibular sense Your sense of balance . It is detected mainly by the fluid-filled semicircular canals in the inner ear, together with structures in the brain. Spin around quickly and stop: the fluid keeps moving, which is why the room seems to keep spinning. Kinesthesis Your sense of your own body movement and position. It lets you move in a coordinated way without looking, like touching your nose with your eyes closed or typing without looking at the keys.

items.x: Bottom-up and top-down processing Bottom-up processing starts with the raw sensory information and builds up to a perception, piece by piece. Top-down processing starts with what you already know and expect, and uses that to interpret the information. Most of the time you use both at once. Try it: is it a letter or a number? Read across, then read down. The middle symbol is exactly the same in both directions. A 12 13 14 C Read across, it looks like the number 13. Read down, between A and C, it looks like the letter B. The marks on the screen did not change; your expectation did. That is top-down processing. What filters your perception Factor Type What it means Example Schemas Internal Mental frameworks that organize what you know about something. Your schema for "classroom" lets you instantly recognize a room you have never been in as one. Perceptual set Internal A readiness to perceive something in a particular way, based on expectations. Told that a song hides a secret message, listeners suddenly "hear" words that were never there. Context External The surroundings change how the same stimulus is interpreted. A shape is read as a letter among letters and a number among numbers. Experience External What you have encountered before tunes what you notice. A chef walking through a spice market spots details a visitor misses. Culture External Cultural experiences and expectations shape interpretation. People raised among straight-edged buildings tend to be more fooled by some line-length illusions.

items.s: Gestalt principles: organizing what you see
items.k: Gestalt principles: organizing what you see | Closure | Figure and ground | Proximity | Similarity | Memory hook
items.x: Gestalt principles: organizing what you see Gestalt psychologists argued that we perceive whole patterns, not separate pieces: the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The CED names four principles that explain how we organize what we see. Closure We fill in gaps to see a complete, whole object. You see a circle, not eight curved lines. Figure and ground We separate an object (the figure) from its background (the ground). Is this a white circle on a dark square, or a dark frame with a hole? Proximity We group things that are close together. You see three groups of four dots, not twelve separate dots. Similarity We group things that look alike. The evenly spaced dots read as rows, because each row shares a color. Memory hook Closure closes gaps. Figure and ground : what stands out and what sits behind. Proximity = nearby belongs together. Similarity = same-looking belongs together.

items.k: Attention | Selective attention and the cocktail party effect | Blindness from inattention | cocktail party effect | Change blindness | Spot the difference | changed
items.x: Attention Attention is where sensation and perception meet. Far more information reaches your senses than you could ever process, so attention selects what gets through, shaped by both internal factors (your goals, your interests) and external ones (a sudden noise, a bright color). Selective attention and the cocktail party effect Focusing on one thing while filtering out the rest. In a loud school cafeteria you can follow one friend's conversation, yet you still notice instantly when someone across the room says your name. That is the cocktail party effect . Filtered out, but not completely ignored. Blindness from inattention When attention is elsewhere, we can miss things that are right in front of us. In a well-known study, many viewers counting basketball passes completely missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the game. Change blindness is a specific form: failing to notice that something in the scene has changed. Looking is not the same as seeing. Spot the difference Missing something new that appears while you are focused elsewhere is blindness from inattention. Failing to notice that something already there has changed (a different person, a moved object, a missing detail between two film shots) is change blindness .

items.x: Depth perception Your retina is a flat surface, yet you see a three-dimensional world. Your brain rebuilds depth from cues. Binocular cues: need both eyes Retinal disparity Each eye sees a slightly different image, and the brain compares them. The bigger the difference, the closer the object. Hold up a finger and close each eye in turn: it jumps. Convergence Your eyes turn inward to focus on something close. The more they turn in, the closer the brain judges the object to be. Bring a finger toward your nose and feel your eyes cross. Monocular cues: work with one eye (and in photos) Monocular cues give an impression of depth even on flat, two-dimensional surfaces like a photo or a painting. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Cue How it signals distance Example Relative clarity Hazy or blurry objects seem farther away than sharp, clear ones. On a humid or dusty day, distant towers look fainter and farther than they really are. Relative size Of two objects you assume are similar in size, the one that looks smaller seems farther away. Two identical palm trees: the smaller-looking one seems farther down the road. Texture gradient Textures look coarse and detailed up close and become finer and denser with distance. Ripples in the sand are clear at your feet and blur into smooth sand toward the horizon. Linear perspective Parallel lines seem to come together in the distance; the closer they get, the farther away it seems. The lanes of a long, straight highway appear to meet at the horizon. Interposition An object that blocks part of another is seen as closer. A car partly hiding a building is seen as in front of it.

items.k: Constancy and apparent movement | Perceptual constancy | Apparent movement
items.x: Constancy and apparent movement Perceptual constancy We keep perceiving an object as the same even when its image on the retina changes. A friend walking away gets smaller on your retina, but you do not think she is shrinking (size constancy). A door swinging open changes shape on your retina, but you still see a rectangle (shape constancy). A white shirt looks white in shade and in sunlight (brightness and color constancy). Stable world, changing images. Apparent movement We can perceive movement where none exists. A film or a phone animation is a rapid series of still images, and a strip of lights switching on and off in sequence looks like a single light moving along. Still images, moving perception.

A perceptual set is often created by what someone was just told or expects to see. Binocular cues Need both eyes: retinal disparity and convergence. Monocular cues Work with one eye and in flat images. If the cue works in a photograph, it must be monocular. Relative size Compares the size of two similar objects. Linear perspective Uses parallel lines that seem to converge. Two similar objects? Relative size. Lines meeting in the distance? Linear perspective. items.x: Concepts, prototypes and schemas Concepts are the mental categories that form the building blocks of thought: "bird", "furniture", "teacher". For each concept we hold a prototype , the best or most typical example. Prototypes can vary with experience: for many people in the UAE, a falcon may come to mind for "bird" faster than it would for someone elsewhere. Schemas are broader frameworks for thinking about how something works. We keep them up to date in two ways: Assimilation Taking in new information and fitting it into an existing schema without changing the schema. A toddler who knows horses sees a camel and calls it a horse. Accommodation Changing the schema to fit new information that does not match. The toddler learns that camels are a separate kind of animal, and creates a new category.

items.k: Solving problems: algorithms and heuristics | Algorithm | Heuristic | Two heuristics that can mislead you | Representativeness heuristic | Availability heuristic
items.x: Solving problems: algorithms and heuristics Algorithm A step-by-step method that tries every possible solution until the right one is found. It guarantees an answer, but can be very slow. Trying every combination of a three-digit lock, from 000 to 999. Heuristic A mental shortcut or rule of thumb. Fast and usually good enough, but it can lead to errors in judgment. Guessing the lock code is the owner's birthday. Two heuristics that can mislead you Representativeness heuristic Judging how likely something is by how well it matches your prototype or stereotype, while ignoring how common it actually is. Assuming a quiet student who loves poetry must study literature, not engineering, even though far more students study engineering. Availability heuristic Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, especially recent or vivid ones. After seeing plane crash footage all week, feeling flying is more dangerous than driving, though driving is far riskier.

items.k: What pushes decisions off course
items.x: What pushes decisions off course Decisions are pulled off course by past experience, by what we have just been exposed to, by how choices are worded and by faulty beliefs about chance and cost. Test yourself: cover the concept column and name the trap from the scenario. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Scenario Concept What is going on A student keeps using a long method from last year's math class, even though this problem has a two-step shortcut. Mental set Sticking with an approach that worked before, even when a better one exists. After a lesson about food, students who are asked to complete "SO_P" are more likely to write SOUP than SOAP. Priming Earlier exposure activates related ideas and nudges later responses, often without awareness. Shoppers prefer yogurt labeled "90 percent fat-free" over one labeled "10 percent fat". Framing The way choices are worded changes decisions, even when the facts are identical. A coin has landed heads five times in a row, so a player bets heavily on tails, sure that it is "due". Gambler's fallacy Believing past random events change the odds of future ones. Mohammed hates a film but stays to the end because he already paid for the ticket. Sunk-cost fallacy Continuing because of what has already been invested, rather than what lies ahead.

items.k: Executive functions and creativity | Divergent thinking | Convergent thinking | Executive functions | Creativity | What blocks creative thinking | Functional fixedness
items.x: Executive functions and creativity Executive functions are the cognitive processes that let you generate, organize, plan and carry out goal-directed behavior and think critically: making a revision timetable, sticking to it, and adjusting when something comes up. (They depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex, Topic 1.4.) Creativity is the ability to produce novel and useful ideas. Divergent thinking Generating many different possible answers. Creativity depends on it. List as many uses for a paperclip as you can in one minute. Convergent thinking Narrowing down to the single best answer. A multiple-choice question with one correct option. What blocks creative thinking Functional fixedness is the tendency to see objects only in terms of their usual function. Needing a screwdriver and not realizing a coin could turn the screw is functional fixedness. It is the opposite of divergent thinking.

items.x: Common mix-ups Availability heuristic How easily examples come to mind. Representativeness heuristic How well something matches a prototype. Ask: is the person recalling vivid examples, or comparing to a stereotype? Assimilation New information fits the old schema; the schema stays the same. Accommodation The schema changes to fit new information. Accommodation is the one where the person changes their mind. Mental set Repeating a strategy that worked before. Functional fixedness Seeing an object only in its usual role. Mental set is about methods; functional fixedness is about objects. Gambler's fallacy Thinks past chance events change future odds. Sunk-cost fallacy Keeps going because of what has already been spent. One is about chance; the other is about investment. Priming Earlier exposure nudges later responses. Framing The wording of the choice changes the decision. Priming happens before; framing is in how the question itself is presented.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do You remember your first day at this school, that Abu Dhabi is the UAE's capital, how to ride a bike, and (hopefully) that your homework is due on Thursday. Those are four very different kinds of memory. This topic sorts them out and introduces the three models psychologists use to explain how memory works. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Tell apart explicit (episodic and semantic), implicit (procedural) and prospective memory. Explain long-term potentiation as a biological basis of memory. Describe the multi-store model, including sensory memory, automatic and effortful processing. Describe the working memory model and its three components. Explain the levels of processing model: structural, phonemic and semantic. How this shows up on the exam Expect to classify a memory from a description ("remembering your cousin's wedding" is episodic) and to identify which model or component a scenario describes. Students often treat the multi-store model and the working memory model as the same thing: they are not.

items.k: Types of memory | Memory | Explicit memory | Episodic memory | Semantic memory | Implicit memory | Procedural memory | Prospective memory | The biology: long-term potentiation | easily describe or explain | experiences and events | Hook | facts and general knowledge | hard to describe or explain | skills and procedures | future actions | Long-term potentiation | Memory hook
items.x: Types of memory Tap a box to see what that kind of memory is. Explicit Episodic Semantic Implicit Procedural Prospective Memory Memories for knowledge, events and experiences differ in how they are processed, stored and retrieved. The main split is between memories you can easily describe (explicit) and those you cannot (implicit). Explicit memory Memory you can consciously recall and easily describe or explain to someone else. Sometimes called declarative memory. It comes in two types: episodic and semantic. Episodic memory Memory for personal experiences and events , tied to a time and place: your first day at this school, what happened at your cousin's wedding. Hook: Episodic = episodes of your life. Semantic memory Memory for facts and general knowledge , not tied to when you learned them: Abu Dhabi is the capital of the UAE; the hippocampus forms new memories. Hook: Semantic = sense and meaning, facts. Implicit memory Memory that shows up in what you do, but is hard to describe or explain in words. You know it without knowing how you know it. Procedural memory A type of implicit memory for skills and procedures : riding a bike, typing on your phone, tying a headscarf or shoelaces. Try explaining exactly how you keep your balance on a bike: it is surprisingly hard. Hook: Procedural = how to do it. Prospective memory Memory for future actions : remembering to submit your homework on Thursday, or to call your grandmother after school. It is remembering to remember. The biology: long-term potentiation Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of synaptic connections between neurons when they are activated together frequently. Each time you practice retrieving a fact, the connection behind it becomes a little easier to activate. It is the biological process thought to underlie memory, and it links back to neural firing in Topic 1.3. Memory hook Neurons that fire together, wire together.

items.x: Three models of memory 1. The multi-store model Information must pass through three interacting systems to be remembered. Most of what hits your senses never makes it past the first one. Sensory memory holds a brief, detailed copy of what your senses take in: iconic memory for sights (a fraction of a second) and echoic memory for sounds (a few seconds; why you can "replay" what someone just said when you weren't listening). What you pay attention to moves into short-term memory , which holds a small amount for a short time. Information that is encoded moves into long-term memory , which is long-lasting and has huge capacity. Retrieval brings it back when you need it. The model highlights two kinds of processing. Automatic processing happens without effort or awareness (you remember roughly where you sat at lunch without trying). Effortful processing needs attention and work (memorizing the stages of sleep). 2. The working memory model This model zooms in on what you are actively doing with information right now. Your working memory is an active workspace with three parts that work together to process information into long-term memory. The central executive directs attention and coordinates the other parts, like a manager. The phonological loop holds sounds and words: repeating a phone number in your head. The visuospatial sketchpad holds images and spatial layouts: picturing the route from your classroom to the library. 3. The levels of processing model How deeply you process information determines how well you remember it, from shallowest to deepest: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Level You focus on... Example question you ask yourself Memory strength Structural What the word looks like Is it written in capital letters? Shallow: weakest Phonemic What the word sounds like Does it rhyme with "sky"? Middle Semantic What the word means Is it a type of feeling, and when did I last feel it? Deep: strongest

"Remembering your graduation" is episodic; "knowing what graduation means" is semantic. Explicit memory Easy to describe in words. Implicit memory Shows in what you do; hard to put into words. Procedural memory is implicit. Short-term memory (multi-store) A temporary store that holds information briefly. Working memory An active workspace that manipulates information. If the scenario involves doing something with information (mental math, picturing a route), think working memory. Automatic processing Encoding without effort or awareness. Effortful processing Encoding that needs attention and work. Both come from the multi-store model. Phonemic processing Focus on sound. Semantic processing Focus on meaning. Semantic is the deepest level and gives the best recall.
