items.k: What you need to be able to do
items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Encoding is getting information into memory in the first place. If it never goes in properly, no amount of last-minute panic will get it out. The good news: how you encode is largely up to you. This topic is the psychology behind the study strategies that actually work. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain mnemonic devices, including the method of loci. Explain how chunking, categories and hierarchies improve encoding. Explain the spacing effect: massed versus distributed practice. Explain the serial position effect, including the primacy and recency effects. How this shows up on the exam Expect a scenario describing how someone studies or what they remember from a list, and a question asking which encoding strategy or effect is at work. This topic also lends itself to data questions, such as reading a serial position graph.

items.k: Mnemonics and organizing information | Mnemonic devices | Organizing information | Chunking | Categories | Hierarchies | Try it: chunking a phone number | method of loci
items.x: Mnemonics and organizing information How information is encoded determines how well it is stored and how easily it can be retrieved later. The CED names several ways to encode more effectively. Mnemonic devices Mnemonic devices are memory aids that help encode information into working and long-term memory: acronyms, rhymes, vivid images. The method of loci is a powerful one: you imagine walking through a familiar place, such as your home, and "place" each item you need to remember in a different spot. To recall them, you take the same walk in your mind. Organizing information Chunking Grouping individual items into meaningful units, so short-term memory holds a few chunks instead of many items. See the phone number below. Categories Sorting items into groups by type. A shopping list grouped into fruit, dairy and bread. Hierarchies Organizing information from broad categories down to specific details. The nervous system map in Topic 1.2: nervous system, then CNS and PNS, then their branches. Try it: chunking a phone number Glance at each version for two seconds, look away, and try to repeat it. 971501234567 +971 50 123 4567 Same twelve digits. The second version is four meaningful chunks (country code, network, then two groups), which is far easier to hold in short-term memory.

items.k: The spacing effect | Massed practice (cramming) | Distributed practice | spacing effect | spread out over time | Use this, don't just learn it
items.x: The spacing effect The spacing effect is the finding that you remember far more when study is spread out over time than when it is crammed into one session, even if the total time is the same. Massed practice (cramming) Studying all at once, such as six hours the night before a test. It can feel productive, and it may get you through tomorrow, but much of it fades quickly. Six hours, one night. Distributed practice Spreading study across several shorter sessions with gaps in between. Each session strengthens the memory and consolidation has time to work. One hour, six times, across two weeks. Use this, don't just learn it Distributed practice is one of the best-supported study strategies in all of psychology. For the AP exam in May, a little Unit 2 review every week will beat a frantic week of cramming in April.

items.k: The serial position effect | Primacy effect | Recency effect | serial position effect | beginning | end
items.x: The serial position effect The order in which information is presented affects how well it is encoded. Read someone a list of fifteen words and ask them to recall as many as they can: they will remember the first few and the last few best, and lose the middle. This is the serial position effect . Primacy effect Items at the beginning are remembered well, because there was time to rehearse them and move them into long-term memory. The first names you hear at a party. Recency effect Items at the end are remembered well, because they are still in short-term memory. The last few things your teacher said before the bell. One extra detail worth knowing: if recall is delayed instead of immediate, the recency effect tends to fade (those items have left short-term memory), while the primacy effect remains.

items.k: Common mix-ups | Primacy effect | Recency effect | Massed practice | Distributed practice | Chunking | Method of loci | first | last
items.x: Common mix-ups Primacy effect Better recall for the first items. Recency effect Better recall for the last items. Primary school comes first; recent events happened last. Massed practice All at once; feels efficient, fades fast. Distributed practice Spread out over time; lasts longer. The spacing effect is the reason distributed practice wins. Chunking Grouping items into meaningful units. Method of loci Placing items along an imagined familiar route. Chunking organizes; the method of loci uses imagery and location.

items.x: Check yourself Answer each one in your head (or out loud) before you open it. 1. To memorize a speech, Salama imagines walking through her house, placing each main point in a different room. Which technique is she using? The method of loci, a mnemonic device that uses a familiar route to encode items in order. 2. You remember a credit card number by reading it as four groups of four digits. Which strategy is this? Chunking. Sixteen separate digits become four meaningful units. 3. items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Some memories vanish in a second; others last a lifetime. This topic compares the different memory stores by how long they last and how much they hold, explains how rehearsal keeps information alive, and looks at what happens when storage itself is damaged. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Compare sensory, short-term, working and long-term memory by duration, capacity and content. Explain maintenance rehearsal and elaborative rehearsal. That last pair is a favorite, so learn which direction each one points.

items.s: How long, how much, what kind
items.k: How long, how much, what kind | Keeping information alive: rehearsal | Maintenance rehearsal | Elaborative rehearsal
items.x: How long, how much, what kind The memory systems from Topic 2.3 differ in three ways: how long they hold information (duration), how much they hold (capacity) and what kind of information they hold (content). Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Store Duration Capacity Content Sensory memory A fraction of a second (sights) to a few seconds (sounds) Large: a brief copy of everything the senses take in Raw sensory information Short-term memory Around 20 to 30 seconds without rehearsal Small: roughly 7 items, give or take 2 Whatever you are paying attention to right now Working memory As long as you keep actively using it Limited Information you are actively manipulating: solving, comparing, planning Long-term memory Minutes to a lifetime Essentially unlimited Knowledge, skills and experiences Keeping information alive: rehearsal Maintenance rehearsal Repeating information over and over to keep it in memory. It prolongs storage, but adds little meaning. Repeating a Wi-Fi password until you have typed it in. Elaborative rehearsal Rehearsing in a way that connects the information to meaning: linking it to what you know, to examples, to your own life. It leads to much better long-term retention. items.k: Superior memory and the self | highly superior autobiographical memory | biological processes | autobiographical memory | ourselves | Make it personal
items.x: Superior memory and the self A small number of people have highly superior autobiographical memory : give them almost any date from their adult life and they can tell you what day of the week it was and what they did. Cases like these suggest there may be biological processes that allow superior memory storage. For everyone else, autobiographical memory (memory for the events of your own life) helps explain a useful pattern: information connected to ourselves is more memorable. Linking a new term to your own experience is a form of elaborative rehearsal, and it works. Make it personal When you learn a new term, ask: "When has this happened to me?" Connecting it to your own life gives it a stronger place in memory.

items.x: When storage breaks down Storage can be damaged by physical injury or illness, and it is limited by development. Retrograde amnesia Loss of memories from before the injury or illness. The person may not remember the weeks leading up to an accident. Retro = backward in time. Anterograde amnesia Inability to form new memories after the injury, while older memories may stay intact. The person may meet you every day and never remember you. Antero = forward in time. Alzheimer's disease A progressive brain disease that gradually destroys memory. It often begins with difficulty forming new memories and, over time, erodes older ones too. Infantile amnesia Most people have almost no memories from before about age 3 or 4. The brain systems needed to store lasting explicit memories are still developing. A developmental limit, not damage.

items.x: Common mix-ups Retrograde amnesia Can't remember the past, before the injury. Anterograde amnesia Can't make new memories after the injury. Draw the timeline: retrograde points back, anterograde points forward. Maintenance rehearsal Repetition; keeps information briefly. Elaborative rehearsal Adds meaning; stores it better long term. If the student links it to examples or their own life, it is elaborative. Short-term memory A brief, small store. Long-term memory A lasting, essentially unlimited store. Short-term memory holds about 7 items; long-term memory has no known limit.

Retrieval is getting information back out of memory, and this topic explains why it sometimes fails and how to make it far more reliable. items.k: Recall and recognition | Recall | Recognition | without cues | retrieval cues
items.x: Recall and recognition Recall Retrieving information without cues : you have to produce it yourself. A fill-in-the-blank question, or a free-response answer. Recognition Identifying information when it is presented to you, using retrieval cues . A multiple-choice question: the right answer is in front of you. Recognition is usually easier than recall, which is why you can recognize a classmate's face years later even if you could never recall their name unprompted.

items.k: Matching the moment | environment | mood | physical state | Clue words | Place | Feeling | Body
items.x: Matching the moment Retrieval improves when your situation at retrieval matches your situation when you encoded the information. The match acts as a retrieval cue. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Effect What has to match Example Context-dependent memory The environment or place You walk into the kitchen and forget why, then remember once you are back at your desk. Mood-congruent memory Your mood When you are feeling low, sad memories come to mind more easily; when happy, happy ones do. State-dependent memory Your physical state Material learned while very tired, or after strong coffee, is recalled better in that same physical state. Clue words Place or room: context. Feeling or emotion: mood. Body or physical condition: state.

items.k: Retrieval practice | The testing effect | Metacognition | Use this before May
items.x: Retrieval practice Successful retrieval becomes more likely with retrieval practice : deliberately pulling information out of memory, rather than just putting it in again. The testing effect Remembering is enhanced by retrieving information, not just rereading it. Testing yourself is a way of learning, not only of checking. Answering practice questions beats highlighting your notes again. Metacognition Thinking about your own thinking: judging what you really know and what you only recognize, then adjusting how you study. "I can recognize these terms, but can I explain them without looking?" Use this before May Rereading feels comfortable, because the material looks familiar. That feeling is recognition, not recall. The practice quizzes on this site use the testing effect, so do them before you feel ready, not after.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Forgetting is not always failure. Your brain is constantly deciding what to keep, and it rebuilds memories every time you recall them. This topic explains why we forget, and why a memory can feel completely certain and still be wrong. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Interpret the forgetting curve. Explain encoding failure, proactive and retroactive interference, and inadequate retrieval (the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon). Explain the psychodynamic idea of repression. Explain the misinformation effect, source amnesia and constructive memory, including imagination inflation. How this shows up on the exam Proactive versus retroactive interference is one of the most tested pairs in the whole course: be sure which direction each one runs. Expect scenarios about eyewitnesses and false memories for the misinformation effect and source amnesia, and graph questions on the forgetting curve.

items.k: The forgetting curve | forgetting curve | quickly, soon after learning | levels off | The study lesson
items.x: The forgetting curve The forgetting curve , first mapped by Hermann Ebbinghaus, shows that time is a major factor in forgetting. Most forgetting happens quickly, soon after learning , and then the curve levels off : what survives the first few days tends to last. The study lesson The steep early drop is why reviewing a lesson within a day or two (distributed practice, Topic 2.4) is so effective: it catches the memory before most of it slips away.

items.k: Why we forget | Repression: a psychodynamic explanation | Old | new | Memory hook for interference | Pro | forward | Retro | back | repression
items.x: Why we forget Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Reason What happens Example Encoding failure The information never got into long-term memory in the first place. You have handled one-dirham coins a thousand times, but could you draw the front from memory? Proactive interference Old learning gets in the way of remembering new information. You keep typing your old password after changing it. Retroactive interference New learning gets in the way of remembering old information. After learning your new class timetable, you cannot remember last year's. Inadequate retrieval The memory is stored, but you cannot access it right now. The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon: you know the actor's name, you know it starts with M, but it will not come. Memory hook for interference Pro active: the old memory moves forward and blocks the new. Retro active: the new memory reaches back and blocks the old. Ask which memory is the one you are failing to remember: if it is the new one, it is proactive. Repression: a psychodynamic explanation Psychodynamic theorists, following Freud, believe some memories are forgotten to protect the ego from distress: the mind pushes painful memories out of conscious awareness. This is called repression . Many researchers question how often this really happens, but you need to know what the psychodynamic perspective claims.

items.k: When memories are wrong | Misinformation effect | Source amnesia | Constructive memory | Imagination inflation | after | where | Why this matters beyond the exam
items.x: When memories are wrong Memory is not a video recording. Each time you recall something, you rebuild it, and the rebuilt version can change. Misinformation effect Misleading information introduced after an event distorts the memory of it. In classic studies, people who were asked how fast cars were going when they "smashed" into each other gave higher speed estimates, and were more likely to falsely remember broken glass, than people asked about cars that "hit" each other. The wording of the question rewrote the memory. Source amnesia Remembering information but forgetting where it came from. You are sure your teacher said a "fact" that you actually saw in a social media video. The content stays; the source fades. Constructive memory Memories are reconstructed each time they are recalled and consolidated again, so gaps get filled with what seems likely. Your memory of a family trip slowly absorbs details from the photos and stories. Imagination inflation Repeatedly imagining an event that never happened increases your confidence that it did. Picturing yourself getting lost as a child can make you more confident it really happened. Why this matters beyond the exam These findings are why psychologists urge caution about eyewitness memory and leading questions: a confident memory is not always an accurate one.

items.k: Common mix-ups | Proactive interference | Retroactive interference | Encoding failure | Inadequate retrieval | Misinformation effect | Source amnesia | Repression | Ordinary forgetting
items.x: Common mix-ups Proactive interference Old blocks new. Retroactive interference New blocks old. Old password typed by mistake: proactive. Forgetting last year's timetable: retroactive. Encoding failure It never went in. Inadequate retrieval It went in, but you can't get it out right now. Tip of the tongue is a retrieval failure, not an encoding failure. Misinformation effect Later information changes the memory itself. Source amnesia The memory is fine; its source is forgotten. Ask whether the content changed or only the source was lost. Repression Forgetting to protect the ego (a psychodynamic idea). Ordinary forgetting Time, interference, encoding or retrieval failure. If the memory is distressing and pushed out of awareness, the answer is repression.

items.s: What you need to be able to do
items.k: What you need to be able to do | Not on the exam
items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do What does it mean to be "smart"? Is it one ability or many? Can a test measure it fairly? And what happens when test scores are used to decide people's futures? This topic covers how psychologists have tried to answer these questions, and where they got it wrong. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain the debate over whether intelligence is a general ability (g) or several abilities. Explain how IQ was calculated, and what makes a test standardized, valid and reliable. Explain stereotype threat, stereotype lift and the Flynn effect. Explain how intelligence scores can be affected by bias and inequity, and how they have been misused. Compare achievement and aptitude tests, and fixed and growth mindsets. How this shows up on the exam Expect questions on psychometrics: which type of reliability or validity a scenario describes, or whether a test is reliable but not valid. You should also be ready to use the Flynn effect and within-group variation to evaluate claims about group differences in IQ. Not on the exam Labeling or describing particular cognitive abilities and disabilities.

items.k: What is intelligence? | One general ability (g) | Multiple abilities | general ability | several different abilities
items.x: What is intelligence? Psychologists still do not agree on exactly how to define intelligence, and definitions and measures have been subject to bias throughout history. The central debate: One general ability (g) Intelligence is a single general ability , called g , that underlies performance on many different tasks. People who do well on one kind of test tend to do well on others. Associated with Charles Spearman. Multiple abilities Intelligence is made up of several different abilities that can be strong or weak independently, such as musical, interpersonal or practical intelligence. Associated with Howard Gardner and Robert Sternberg. (The CED does not require the theorists' names, but they often appear in questions and textbooks.)

items.k: Measuring intelligence | Try it: the original IQ formula | What makes a test useful? | mental age | chronological age | identify students for educational services | psychometric | Construct validity | Predictive validity | Test-retest | Split-half | The bathroom scale test | reliable | not valid
items.x: Measuring intelligence Try it: the original IQ formula Early tests compared a child's mental age (the age level they performed at) with their chronological age (their actual age). Mental age Chronological age IQ = mental age ÷ chronological age × 100. Modern tests no longer use this formula; they compare your score with others your age, with 100 set as the average. Today, IQ scores are often used to identify students for educational services , such as extra support or advanced programs. What makes a test useful? Every psychological test, intelligence tests included, should follow sound psychometric principles. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Principle Meaning Types you need to know Standardized Given and scored using the same procedures and conditions for everyone, so scores can be compared fairly. Same instructions, same time limit, same scoring rules Valid Measures what it claims to measure. Construct validity : does it really measure the idea (the construct) it is meant to? Predictive validity : does it predict the future behavior it should, such as success at university? Reliable Gives consistent results each time. Test-retest : similar scores when the same people take it again later. Split-half : the two halves of the test (say, odd and even questions) give similar scores. The bathroom scale test A scale that always shows you 5 kg heavier than you really are is reliable (same reading every time) but not valid (wrong reading). A test can be reliable without being valid, but it cannot be valid without being reliable.

items.k: Fairness, bias and misuse | Stereotype threat | Stereotype lift | Systemic issues in intelligence testing | socio-culturally responsive | The Flynn effect | societal factors | Variation within and between groups | within | between | Inequity | Misuse | Using these on the exam
items.x: Fairness, bias and misuse Stereotype threat Worry about confirming a negative stereotype about your group can lower your performance. For example, older adults who are reminded beforehand that memory declines with age tend to score lower on a memory test. The worry itself uses up attention. Stereotype lift A performance boost that can come from being compared with a group that is negatively stereotyped. It can widen gaps in scores that have nothing to do with ability. The flip side of threat. For these reasons, researchers try to develop intelligence tests that are socio-culturally responsive , reducing stereotype threat and the unfair gaps that stereotype lift can create. Systemic issues in intelligence testing The Flynn effect: average IQ scores across much of the world have risen over the past century. Genes cannot change that fast, so the rise points to societal factors such as better nutrition, better health care and higher living standards. Variation within and between groups: IQ scores vary more within any group than between groups. Personal and sociocultural biases can affect how an individual's score is interpreted. Inequity: poverty, discrimination and unequal access to education can lower the intelligence scores of individuals and groups around the world. Misuse: intelligence test scores have been used to limit people's access to jobs, military ranks, educational institutions and immigration to the United States. Using these on the exam If a claim says differences in average IQ between two groups must be genetic, the Flynn effect and the role of poverty, discrimination and educational inequity give you strong evidence to challenge it.

items.k: Achievement, aptitude and mindset | Achievement test | Aptitude test | Fixed mindset | Growth mindset | already learned | learn or perform in the future | yet
items.x: Achievement, aptitude and mindset Achievement test Measures what you have already learned . Your AP Psychology exam, or a driving theory test. Aptitude test Predicts how well you will learn or perform in the future . A test that predicts how quickly someone could learn a new language. Fixed mindset The belief that intelligence is set from birth and cannot change much. "I'm just not a science person." Growth mindset The belief that intelligence can grow through effort, strategies and experience. "I'm not good at this yet ." These beliefs matter: students' views about whether intelligence is fixed or can grow are linked to their academic achievement, partly because they shape how students respond to difficulty and mistakes.

items.k: Common mix-ups | Reliability | Validity | Test-retest reliability | Split-half reliability | Construct validity | Predictive validity | Achievement test | Aptitude test | Stereotype threat | Stereotype lift
items.x: Common mix-ups Reliability Consistent results. Validity Measures what it claims to. Reliable but not valid is possible; valid but not reliable is not. Test-retest reliability Same people, same test, two different times. Split-half reliability Comparing two halves of one test. Two sittings: test-retest. One sitting split in two: split-half. Construct validity Does it measure the intended concept? Predictive validity Does it predict future performance? "Predicts" in the question usually signals predictive validity. Achievement test What you know now. Aptitude test What you could do in the future. End-of-unit tests are achievement tests. Stereotype threat Fear of confirming a stereotype lowers performance. Stereotype lift Comparison with a stereotyped group raises performance. Threat pulls down; lift pushes up.

items.x: Check yourself Answer each one in your head (or out loud) before you open it. 1. An 8-year-old performs at the level of a typical 10-year-old. Using the original formula, what is her IQ? 125. Mental age 10 divided by chronological age 8, times 100. 2. Students who take the same test twice, two weeks apart, get very similar scores. What does this show? Test-retest reliability. The test gives consistent results over time. 3. A university entrance test turns out to predict students' first-year grades well. Which kind of validity is this? Predictive validity: the test predicts the future performance it is meant to. 4. A test of "leadership ability" turns out to measure mostly how fast people can read. What is the problem? Poor construct validity. It is not measuring the concept it claims to measure. 5. Average IQ scores in many countries rose sharply over the twentieth century. What is this called, and what does it suggest? The Flynn effect. The rise was too fast for genes, so it points to societal factors such as nutrition, health care and education. 6. After failing a quiz, Abdulla says, "I'll never be good at math, my brain just isn't built for it." Which mindset is this, and why might it matter? A fixed mindset. Believing ability cannot change can lead students to give up, which is linked to lower achievement. items.k: What you need to be able to do
items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Look at a photo of yourself at age five. In some ways you are a completely different person; in others, you are obviously still you. Developmental psychology studies how people grow and change across the whole lifespan, and this topic introduces the big questions it keeps asking and the two main ways it studies change. These notes cover Topics 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4 to 3.9. Topic 3.3 is not part of these materials. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain the difference between studying development in chronological order and by theme. Explain the three enduring themes: stability and change, nature and nurture, and continuous and discontinuous development. Compare cross-sectional and longitudinal research designs, including their strengths and weaknesses. How this shows up on the exam Expect to identify a theme from a research question ("Do shy toddlers become shy adults?" is stability and change) and to identify or evaluate a research design. The classic trap is forgetting that cross-sectional studies can be distorted by cohort effects, while longitudinal studies lose participants over time.

items.t: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology
items.k: Three enduring themes | chronological order | theme | Picture it | Continuous | Discontinuous
items.x: Three enduring themes Developmental psychologists study development in two ways: in chronological order (infancy, then childhood, then adolescence, and so on) and by theme (big questions that run across every age). Three themes come up again and again: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Theme The question it asks Example research question Stability and change Which traits stay the same across life, and which change? Will a shy toddler become a shy adult? Nature and nurture How do genes and experience interact to shape development? (Topic 1.1) Is a child's talent for languages inherited, or the result of growing up bilingual? Continuous and discontinuous development Does development happen gradually and steadily (continuous), or in distinct stages with sudden shifts (discontinuous)? Do children's thinking skills improve a little every day, or jump from one stage to the next? Picture it Continuous development is a ramp: a smooth, steady climb. Discontinuous development is a staircase: flat stretches, then a step up to a new stage. Piaget's theory (Topic 3.4) and Erikson's (Topic 3.6) are staircases.

items.t: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology
items.k: Cross-sectional and longitudinal designs | Cross-sectional design | Longitudinal design | different people of different ages | one point in time | Weakness | cohort effect | the same people | repeatedly over a long time | Weaknesses | attrition | Classic trap
items.x: Cross-sectional and longitudinal designs To study change over time, researchers use two main designs. Cross-sectional design Compares different people of different ages at one point in time . Quick and inexpensive. Weakness: the cohort effect . People born in different eras grew up with different schooling, technology and culture, so age differences may really be generation differences. Test 20-, 40- and 60-year-olds this week. Longitudinal design Follows the same people and tests them repeatedly over a long time . Shows real change within individuals. Weaknesses: slow and expensive, and attrition : participants drop out over the years, and the ones who stay may not be typical. Test the same group at ages 20, 40 and 60. Classic trap A cross-sectional study finds that older adults score lower on a computer-based problem-solving test than young adults. Before concluding that problem-solving declines with age, ask: did the older group grow up with computers? That is a cohort effect, and a longitudinal design avoids it.

items.t: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology
items.k: Common mix-ups | Cross-sectional | Longitudinal | Cohort effect | Attrition | Stability and change | Continuous and discontinuous
items.x: Common mix-ups Cross-sectional Different people, different ages, one time. Longitudinal Same people, tested many times, over years. Same people over time? Longitudinal. One snapshot of many ages? Cross-sectional. Cohort effect A weakness of cross-sectional designs: generation, not age, explains the difference. Attrition A weakness of longitudinal designs: participants drop out. Match each weakness to its design. Stability and change Does a trait persist across life? Continuous and discontinuous Is change gradual, or in stages? Both are about change over time; ask whether the question is about a trait lasting or about the pattern of change.

items.t: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology
items.k: Check yourself | Can you... | Stability and change | Cross-sectional | The cohort effect | Attrition | Discontinuous
items.x: Check yourself Answer each one in your head (or out loud) before you open it. 1. A researcher asks whether children who are anxious at age 3 are still anxious at age 30. Which theme is this? Stability and change. The question is whether a trait persists across the lifespan. 2. To study memory and age, a team tests 500 people aged 20 to 80 in a single month. Which design is this? Cross-sectional. Different people of different ages are compared at one point in time. 3. In that study, the oldest group performs worst on a smartphone-based memory test. Why might that not prove that memory declines with age? The cohort effect. The oldest group grew up without smartphones, so unfamiliarity with the device, not age itself, could explain the difference. 4. A study follows 1,000 babies until age 40. By the end, only 400 are still taking part. What problem does this create? Attrition. The people who stayed may differ from those who left, which can bias the results of a longitudinal study. 5. A theory says children's thinking moves through four distinct stages, each very different from the last. Continuous or discontinuous? Discontinuous. Development happens in distinct stages, like steps on a staircase. items.x: Before birth Before birth, several factors can influence the major physical and psychological milestones of development: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. items.x: Infancy and childhood Physical development in infancy and childhood follows generally the same order for everyone, but the timing varies from child to child. These skills let children become steadily more independent. Gross motor skills Large movements using big muscle groups. Rolling over, sitting up, crawling, walking, kicking a ball. Fine motor skills Small, precise movements, especially of the hands and fingers. Picking up a raisin, holding a crayon, buttoning a shirt. Reflexes and early research Infant reflexes are automatic responses that show development is on track. In the rooting reflex , a baby turns toward a touch on the cheek and opens its mouth, ready to feed. The visual cliff is a glass-topped table with a checkered pattern that appears to drop away halfway across. Most crawling babies refuse to cross the "drop", even when a parent calls them, showing they can perceive depth early in life. It was also an inventive way to study babies who cannot yet answer questions. Critical and sensitive periods Critical period A strict window early in life when a certain experience must happen for normal development. Some animals imprint : newly hatched ducklings and geese follow the first moving object they see, normally their mother, which helps them survive. Sensitive period A window when learning a skill is much easier , but still possible later. Children pick up a second language with a native accent far more easily than adults do.

items.k: Adolescence and adulthood | Adolescence | Adulthood | adolescent growth spurt | puberty | Primary sex characteristics | Secondary sex characteristics | Menarche | spermarche | level off | gradually decline | menopause | Think behavior, not just biology
items.x: Adolescence and adulthood Adolescence Adolescence brings the adolescent growth spurt (a rapid increase in height and weight) and puberty , the period when the body matures and reproductive ability develops. Primary sex characteristics are the body structures directly involved in reproduction. Secondary sex characteristics are other physical changes of puberty that are not directly involved in reproduction, such as a deepening voice or the growth of body hair. Menarche (a girl's first menstrual period) and spermarche (a boy's first ejaculation) are milestones that mark the development of reproductive ability. Adulthood Adulthood is most of the lifespan. Physical abilities generally level off and then gradually decline , at different rates for different people. Changes include: a decline in reproductive ability, including menopause , the end of menstruation; reduced mobility and flexibility; slower reaction time; less sharp vision and hearing. Think behavior, not just biology The exam asks how physical changes relate to behavior. Slower reaction times can affect how safely an older adult drives; the growth spurt can affect a teenager's coordination in sport for a while.

items.k: Common mix-ups | Critical period | Sensitive period | Gross motor skills | Fine motor skills | Primary sex characteristics | Secondary sex characteristics
items.x: Common mix-ups Critical period The experience must happen in this window. Sensitive period Learning is easiest in this window, but possible later. Imprinting is the classic critical period; language is usually described as a sensitive period. Gross motor skills Large movements: crawling, walking. Fine motor skills Small, precise movements: holding a pencil. Big muscles versus small muscles. Primary sex characteristics Directly involved in reproduction. Secondary sex characteristics Other changes of puberty, not directly reproductive. A deepening voice is secondary.

items.k: Piaget: four stages of thinking | Assimilation | Accommodation | Sensorimotor stage (infancy to toddlerhood) | Preoperational stage (toddlerhood to early childhood) | Concrete operational stage (early to late childhood) | Formal operational stage (late childhood through adulthood) | schemas | continuous | discontinuous | senses and actions | object permanence | mental symbols | pretend play | cannot | No conservation | No reversibility | Animism | Egocentrism | theory of mind | correct the errors | struggle to think systematically | abstractly and hypothetically | not everyone
items.x: Piaget: four stages of thinking Jean Piaget argued that children actively build their understanding of the world through schemas , mental frameworks that organize experience. They update them in two ways (you met these in Topic 2.2): Assimilation Fitting new information into an existing schema without changing it. A toddler sees a camel and calls it a horse. Accommodation Changing a schema to fit new information. She learns that camels are a different animal. Piaget saw development as both continuous (schemas are constantly being adjusted) and discontinuous (thinking moves through four distinct stages). Tap a stage to explore it. Sensorimotor Preoperational Concrete operational Formal operational Sensorimotor stage (infancy to toddlerhood) Babies learn about the world through their senses and actions : looking, grabbing, mouthing, dropping. The key achievement is object permanence , understanding that things still exist when you cannot see them. Before it develops, out of sight really is out of mind, which is why peek-a-boo is so thrilling. Preoperational stage (toddlerhood to early childhood) Children become skilled at using mental symbols : words, images and pretend play (a banana becomes a phone). The stage is known more for what children cannot yet do, and the errors they make: No conservation: pour juice from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin one, and the child says there is now more. No reversibility: they cannot mentally undo an action (pour the juice back). Animism: believing objects have feelings ("the table hurt me"). Egocentrism: difficulty seeing things from someone else's point of view. Children begin to develop a theory of mind in this stage: understanding that other people have thoughts and beliefs different from their own. Concrete operational stage (early to late childhood) Children can now correct the errors of the preoperational stage: they understand conservation and reversibility, and think logically about real, concrete situations. But they still struggle to think systematically about abstract or hypothetical ideas. Formal operational stage (late childhood through adulthood) People gain the ability to think abstractly and hypothetically : reasoning about "what if?" questions, justice, or ideas they have never experienced, and testing possibilities systematically. Piaget proposed that not everyone reaches formal operational thinking.

items.x: Vygotsky: learning with others Lev Vygotsky emphasized that children are social learners . They learn by interacting with other people, within their culture. The zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with guidance. Ideally, learning happens here. Scaffolding is the temporary support a more skilled person gives within the ZPD: hints, questions, demonstrations. Like scaffolding on a building, it is gradually removed as the learner becomes independent. Piaget versus Vygotsky Piaget pictured the child as a little scientist , discovering the world mostly alone. Vygotsky pictured the child as an apprentice , learning alongside more skilled people.

items.x: Thinking in adulthood Thinking keeps changing in adulthood, in two different directions: Crystallized intelligence Your accumulated knowledge, vocabulary and skills. It stays relatively stable through adulthood and can keep growing. An older professor's vast knowledge of her subject. Fluid intelligence Your ability to reason quickly and solve new problems. It tends to decline as people age. Learning a brand-new app quickly. Dementia is a cognitive disorder affecting adults, marked by a decline in memory and thinking severe enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's disease (Topic 2.5) is a common cause.

items.x: The building blocks of language Language is a shared system of arbitrary symbols, combined according to rules, that can produce an endless number of ideas. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Building block What it is Example Phoneme The smallest unit of sound in a language. The sounds b, a and t in "bat". Arabic has phonemes English does not, such as the sound of the letter ع (ayn). Morpheme The smallest unit of meaning . "Unhelpful" has three: un + help + ful. The "s" in "cats" is a morpheme meaning "more than one". Semantics The rules for deriving meaning from words and sentences. Knowing that "-ed" means something happened in the past. items.x: Ecological systems theory Urie Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory explains how the social environment influences development, using five nested systems. Tap a ring to explore it. Microsystem Mesosystem Exosystem Macrosystem Chronosystem Microsystem The groups that have direct contact with you: your family, friends, teachers, classmates, sports team. Mesosystem The relationships between the groups in your microsystem. Your parents meeting your teachers at a parent conference, or your friends getting along (or not) with your family. Exosystem Indirect factors : settings you are not part of that still affect you. Your father's workplace changing his hours, so he is home less; a local decision about funding for your school. Macrosystem The wider culture and cultural events that affect you and everyone around you: shared values (such as respect for elders), the economy, a pandemic that closes schools. Chronosystem Your current stage of life , and how the timing of events across your life shapes their effect. Moving to a new country affects a 6-year-old differently from a 16-year-old. Meso or exo? Mesosystem : two of your settings interacting (home and school). Exosystem : a setting you are not in that still reaches you (a parent's job).

items.x: Peers, identity and adulthood Childhood and adolescence Young children engage with peers through play: parallel play (playing side by side without really interacting, typical of toddlers) and pretend play (acting out roles and imaginary situations). Adolescents rely more and more on their peers. They also show a special type of egocentrism: the imaginary audience : feeling that everyone is watching and judging you ("Everyone noticed my bad hair today"); the personal fable : believing your experiences are unique and that bad things will not happen to you ("No one has ever felt what I feel"; "I won't get hurt"). Identity Adolescents develop a sense of who they will be as adults. One model describes four identity statuses , based on whether a person has explored options and whether they have committed to one: Has made a commitment Has not made a commitment Has explored options Achievement : explored, then chose. "I tried several subjects and chose engineering because it suits me." Moratorium : actively exploring, not yet decided. "I'm trying out different clubs to see what fits." Has not explored Foreclosure : committed without exploring, often to others' expectations. "I'll be a doctor because my family expects it." Diffusion : neither exploring nor committed. "I don't really think about it." Identity has many parts, such as occupational, family, religious and ethnic identity. Young people often develop them by imagining their possible selves : who they might become, or fear becoming. Adulthood Culture shapes when adulthood begins and when major life events (finishing study, starting work, marrying, having children) are expected. This culturally expected timetable is the social clock . Some cultures allow a period of emerging adulthood , roughly from the late teens to the mid-twenties, as a transition between adolescence and full adult responsibility. Adults form families or family-like relationships that should provide mutual support and care. Childhood attachment styles can affect how adults form attachments to other adults.

items.x: How classical conditioning works The behavioral perspective grew out of research on learning through conditioning. Behaviorists traditionally focused on observable behavior and left out mental processes they could not observe directly. Classical conditioning is learning to associate two stimuli, so that one starts to trigger a response the other already produced. Ivan Pavlov discovered it when his dogs began to drool at the sound that came before their food. Here is a version closer to home: 1. Before conditioning Karak (UCS) makes Reem's mouth water (UCR). The kettle whistle is a neutral stimulus (NS): it causes no watering. 2. During conditioning Every afternoon, the whistle (NS) sounds just before the karak (UCS) arrives, and her mouth waters (UCR). Repeated pairings: acquisition. 3. After conditioning Now the whistle alone (CS) makes her mouth water (CR). The NS has become a conditioned stimulus. The whistle, at first Conditioned stimulus (CS) The former NS, which now triggers the response after being paired with the UCS. The whistle, after conditioning Conditioned response (CR) The learned response to the CS. Mouth watering at the whistle The labeling routine 1. What caused the response before any learning ? That is the UCS, and the response is the UCR. 2. What was paired with it? That is the NS, which becomes the CS. 3. The same response, now triggered by the CS, is the CR. items.x: Acquisition, extinction and more Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Process What happens In Reem's case Acquisition The association is learned through repeated pairings. Order matters: the NS should come just before the UCS. Whistle, then karak, many times. Extinction The CR fades when the CS keeps appearing without the UCS. Her family switches to an electric kettle for coffee only; the whistle no longer means karak, and the watering stops. Spontaneous recovery After a rest, an extinguished CR suddenly reappears (usually weaker) when the CS returns. Months later at her grandmother's, the old whistle makes her mouth water again. Generalization Stimuli similar to the CS also trigger the CR. A similar whistle on a TV show makes her mouth water. Discrimination Learning to respond only to the CS, not to similar stimuli. Only her grandmother's particular kettle does it. Higher-order conditioning A CS is used like a UCS to condition a new stimulus. Her grandmother's car always arrives just before the whistle; now the car's sound alone makes her mouth water. Extinction is not erasing Spontaneous recovery shows that extinction suppresses the response rather than deleting the association.

items.x: Emotions, therapy and biological limits Conditioned emotions Emotional responses can be classically conditioned. In a famous and now-criticized study, John Watson and Rosalie Rayner conditioned an infant known as "Little Albert" to fear a white rat by pairing it with a sudden loud noise. The fear generalized to other furry objects. Today the study is a classic example of research that would break ethical guidelines, because it deliberately caused distress to a child and did not remove the fear afterwards. The same principle is used to help people. Counterconditioning replaces an unwanted conditioned response with a new one: a person afraid of dogs is gradually exposed to dogs while feeling calm and relaxed, until the dogs become linked with calm instead of fear. Therapies for many disorders build on this (Unit 5). Biology sets limits Taste aversion A strong dislike of a food after it was followed by illness. It shows one-trial learning (one pairing is enough, and further pairings do not strengthen it) and works even when the illness comes hours later. Sick after a seafood dinner once? You may avoid that dish for years. Biological preparedness Animals are biologically predisposed to learn some associations much more easily than others: taste with illness, or fear of snakes and heights, because these helped survival. Rats link sickness to a taste, not to a light or a sound. Habituation is a related form of learning: a reduced response to a stimulus that is repeated or continues without consequence. You stop jumping at the construction noise next door after a few days.

items.x: Consequences shape behavior In operant conditioning , we learn to associate a behavior with its consequences. Edward Thorndike's Law of Effect states that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to be repeated, and behaviors followed by unpleasant consequences are less likely. B. F. Skinner built on this to study how consequences shape behavior. Behavior increases: reinforcement Behavior decreases: punishment Something added: positive Positive reinforcement Adding something pleasant. A student gets praise for a thoughtful answer, so she answers more often. Positive punishment Adding something unpleasant. Extra chores after breaking curfew. Something removed: negative Negative reinforcement Removing something unpleasant. The car's beeping stops when you buckle your seatbelt, so you buckle up sooner next time. Negative punishment Removing something pleasant. Phone taken away for the weekend after a rude message. Positive and negative are math, not good and bad Positive means add (+). Negative means subtract (minus). Taking a pain reliever because it removes a headache is negative reinforcement: something unpleasant is subtracted, and you are more likely to take it next time. Primary reinforcers Satisfy biological needs, with no learning required. Food, water, warmth. Secondary reinforcers Gain their power through association with primary reinforcers. Money, grades, stars on a chart, a coach's praise. Reinforcement discrimination is learning that a behavior is reinforced in one situation but not another (asking for sweets works with grandma, not with mom). Reinforcement generalization is repeating a reinforced behavior in similar situations (saying "please" everywhere because it worked at home).

Concept What it is Example Shaping Gradually teaching a complex behavior by reinforcing successive approximations : each small step closer to the goal. Falconers train a falcon by rewarding it for flying a short distance to the glove, then gradually lengthening the distance. Instinctive drift Animals drift back toward natural, instinctive behaviors, which limits what can be shaped. Raccoons trained to drop coins in a box kept rubbing the coins together, as they would wash food. Superstitious behavior A behavior is accidentally reinforced by a consequence it did not cause. A player scores while wearing particular socks and now wears them for every match. Learned helplessness After repeatedly failing to escape aversive situations, an organism learns it has no control and stops trying, even when escape becomes possible. The fastest way to learn a new behavior, but it also fades fastest once reinforcement stops. A treat every time the puppy sits. Partial reinforcement Only some behaviors are reinforced. Learning is slower, but the behavior is much more resistant to extinction . A treat only some of the times. Partial schedules differ in two ways: is reinforcement based on number of responses (ratio) or time (interval) ? And is it predictable (fixed) or unpredictable (variable) ? Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Schedule Reinforcement comes... Response pattern Example Fixed ratio After a set number of responses High rate, with a short pause after each reward (staircase) A coffee shop card: buy nine, the tenth is free. Variable ratio After an unpredictable number of responses Highest, steadiest rate; the most resistant to extinction Checking your phone for new messages; casting a fishing line. Fixed interval For the first response after a set time Slow after each reward, speeding up as the time approaches (scalloped) Studying hard only just before a quiz every Friday. Variable interval For the first response after an unpredictable time Slow, steady rate Pop quizzes at random times keep students studying steadily. items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do You probably learned to tie your shoes by watching someone, not by being rewarded step by step. And you know the way around your neighborhood even though nobody ever trained you. This topic covers the kinds of learning that classical and operant conditioning cannot fully explain. items.k: Learning by watching | social learning theory | observation | Modeling | Vicarious conditioning | more similar | Bobo doll
items.x: Learning by watching Albert Bandura's social learning theory proposes that we can learn by observation , without personally experiencing a consequence. Modeling: we learn by watching and copying the behavior of others (models). Vicarious conditioning: we learn from the consequences that others receive. Seeing a classmate praised for a creative answer (vicarious reinforcement) makes you more likely to try one; seeing a teammate benched for arguing with the referee (vicarious punishment) makes you less likely to argue. The more similar a model is to us, the more likely we are to learn from them. In Bandura's Bobo doll experiments, children who watched an adult hit and kick an inflatable doll were much more likely to attack the doll themselves, often copying the adult's exact actions and words.

items.t: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning
items.k: Cognitive factors in learning | Insight learning | Latent learning | How the types of learning compare | suddenly | without reinforcement | cognitive map | neurological
items.x: Cognitive factors in learning Insight learning The solution to a problem appears suddenly , without trial and error, reinforcement or a model: the "aha!" moment. Wolfgang Köhler described a chimpanzee named Sultan who, after failing to reach bananas, suddenly stacked boxes and used a stick to get them. A puzzle you stared at for ages, then suddenly saw the answer. Latent learning Learning that happens without reinforcement and stays hidden until there is a reason to show it. Edward Tolman found that rats who explored a maze without food later ran it as fast as rats trained with food, as soon as food was added. They had formed a cognitive map , a mental picture of the layout. Being driven to school for years, then easily giving directions when a friend needs them. These kinds of learning also have a neurological side. Learning strengthens connections between neurons through long-term potentiation (Topic 2.3) and reshapes the brain through plasticity (Topic 1.4). How the types of learning compare Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Type of learning Needs reinforcement? Needs a model? Key example Classical conditioning (3.7) No: it pairs two stimuli No A whistle makes your mouth water. Operant conditioning (3.8) Yes: consequences drive it No Studying more after praise. Observational learning Not directly: others' consequences can matter Yes Bobo doll. Insight learning No No Köhler's chimpanzee stacking boxes. Latent learning Not to learn; only to show it No Tolman's rats and cognitive maps.

Vicarious reinforcement Seeing someone else rewarded makes you more likely to copy. Positive reinforcement (3.8) You are rewarded yourself. Vicarious means it happened to someone else. Observational learning Learning by watching a model. Operant conditioning Learning from your own consequences. If the learner never personally received a consequence, think observational.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do A classmate walks past without saying hello. Is she rude, or did she just get bad news? We explain other people's behavior all day long, usually without noticing, and our explanations are often biased in predictable ways. This topic is about how we explain behavior and how we judge ourselves and others. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Tell dispositional and situational attributions apart, and explain optimistic and pessimistic explanatory styles. Explain the actor/observer bias, the fundamental attribution error and the self-serving bias. Explain internal and external locus of control. Explain the mere exposure effect, the self-fulfilling prophecy, social comparison (upward and downward) and relative deprivation. How this shows up on the exam The three attribution biases are a favorite. They have different targets: the fundamental attribution error is about judging others ; the actor/observer bias contrasts how we explain ourselves versus others ; the self-serving bias is about protecting our self-image .

items.k: Explaining behavior | Dispositional attribution | Situational attribution | Explanatory style | Optimistic explanatory style | Pessimistic explanatory style | Biased explanations | attribution | internal qualities | external circumstances | other people | your own | others'
items.x: Explaining behavior An attribution is how we explain behavior, our own and other people's. Dispositional attribution Explaining behavior by internal qualities : personality, intelligence, effort. "She didn't say hello because she's rude." Situational attribution Explaining behavior by external circumstances . "She didn't say hello because she just got bad news." Explanatory style People show a predictable pattern in how they explain good and bad events: their explanatory style . Optimistic explanatory style Bad events are explained as temporary, specific and not entirely your fault; good events as lasting and earned. "I failed this quiz because I didn't review the right chapter. Next time I will." Pessimistic explanatory style Bad events are explained as permanent, affecting everything, and your fault. "I failed because I'm useless at everything, and I always will be." Biased explanations Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Bias What it is Example Fundamental attribution error Overestimating dispositional causes and underestimating situational ones when judging other people . A driver cuts you off: "What a selfish person." (Maybe they are rushing to the hospital.) Actor/observer bias Explaining your own behavior by the situation, but others' by their disposition. "I was late because of traffic. He was late because he's disorganized." Self-serving bias Taking credit for successes (dispositional) and blaming failures on the situation, to protect self-esteem. "I got an A because I'm smart. I got a C because the test was unfair."

items.k: Locus of control | Internal locus of control | External locus of control
items.x: Locus of control Internal locus of control Believing you control what happens to you, through your own effort and choices. "If I revise properly, I'll do well." External locus of control Believing outside forces (luck, fate, other people) control what happens to you. "It doesn't matter how much I revise; it depends on which questions come up." People with a stronger internal locus of control tend to put in more effort and cope better with setbacks, because they believe their actions make a difference.

items.x: Person perception Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Concept What it is Example Mere exposure effect Being exposed to something repeatedly makes us like it more. A song you disliked at first grows on you after hearing it every day in the car. Self-fulfilling prophecy Our beliefs about someone lead us to act in ways that make those beliefs come true. A teacher who expects a student to do well gives her more attention and encouragement, and she does do well. Upward social comparison Comparing yourself with someone who seems better off. Comparing your grades with the top student in the year: motivating, or discouraging. Downward social comparison Comparing yourself with someone who seems worse off. Feeling better about your mark after hearing others found the test harder. Relative deprivation Feeling deprived compared with others, even when you are well off in absolute terms. Feeling your phone is old and embarrassing because all your friends have the newest model. Social comparison is evaluating yourself by comparing yourself with others in society or in your social circles. Social media makes upward comparison almost constant, which is one reason it can leave people feeling worse about their own lives.

items.x: Common mix-ups Fundamental attribution error Judging others by disposition, ignoring the situation. Actor/observer bias Me : the situation. Them : their disposition. If the scenario compares the person's own behavior with someone else's, it is actor/observer. Self-serving bias Success is mine; failure is the situation's. Explanatory style A general habit of explaining good and bad events. Self-serving bias is about protecting self-esteem in a single judgment. Internal locus of control "My actions decide what happens." External locus of control "Luck or others decide what happens." Listen for who the person credits: themselves, or outside forces. items.s: What you need to be able to do

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do We all carry mental shortcuts about groups of people. That is partly just how memory works: categories help us process the world faster. The problem starts when those categories harden into attitudes, and the attitudes harden into actions. This topic is about how that happens, and why attitudes are so hard to change. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination, and how they are connected. Explain implicit attitudes, the just-world phenomenon, out-group homogeneity bias, in-group bias and ethnocentrism. Explain belief perseverance, confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance. How this shows up on the exam Expect scenarios asking you to tell a belief (stereotype) from a feeling (prejudice) from an action (discrimination), and to spot the bias in a group judgment. A useful contrast: cognitive dissonance pushes attitudes to change, while belief perseverance resists change.

items.k: Stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination | Implicit attitudes | belief | feeling | action | Think, feel, act | think | feel
items.x: Stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. What it is Example Stereotype A belief (thought) about a group. Stereotypes reduce mental effort but can be biased, and they often lead to prejudice. "Students from that school are all arrogant." Prejudice A feeling , usually negative, toward a group. Disliking students from that school before meeting any of them. Discrimination An action toward someone because of their group. Refusing to partner with anyone from that school in a project. Think, feel, act Stereotype = what you think . Prejudice = what you feel . Discrimination = what you do . Implicit attitudes Implicit attitudes are attitudes we hold but may not be aware of, or may not admit, even to ourselves. Researchers have shown how they appear as negative judgments of others: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Concept What it is Example Just-world phenomenon Believing the world is fair, so people get what they deserve. It leads to blaming people for their own misfortune. A classmate leaves a demanding program, and others assume she simply didn't try hard enough, without knowing what she was dealing with. Out-group homogeneity bias Seeing members of other groups as all the same, while seeing your own group as varied. "Fans of that football club are all the same," while your own club's fans are "all different kinds of people". In-group bias Favoring your own group. A referee's call seems fair when it helps your team and outrageous when it doesn't. Ethnocentrism Judging other cultures by the standards of your own, as if yours is the normal or correct way. Assuming the way your family does things (shoes on or off indoors) is simply the right way.

items.k: Why attitudes resist change | Belief perseverance | Cognitive dissonance | confirmation bias | Change versus resist | for | against
items.x: Why attitudes resist change When people meet evidence that contradicts a belief they care about, they often do not change the belief. They attack the evidence. Belief perseverance Holding on to a belief even after evidence shows it is wrong. It is often kept alive by confirmation bias : noticing and remembering only the information that supports it. A student insists rereading is the best way to study, even after seeing research that shows it is one of the least effective methods. Cognitive dissonance The mental discomfort we feel when our actions and attitudes conflict. To reduce it, we change either the action or the attitude so they line up again. A student who sees himself as honest copies homework under pressure. He either confesses (changes the action) or tells himself "it was just once, everyone does it" (changes the attitude). Change versus resist Cognitive dissonance is a force for attitude change (to match behavior). Belief perseverance is a force against change (despite evidence).

items.x: Common mix-ups Prejudice A feeling toward a group. Discrimination An action toward a group. Prejudice can exist without discrimination; discrimination is the behavior. Out-group homogeneity bias "They're all the same." In-group bias "We're better." One is about seeing sameness; the other is about favoring your side. Belief perseverance Holding on to a belief despite evidence. Confirmation bias Seeking information that supports a belief. Confirmation bias is often how belief perseverance is maintained. Just-world phenomenon People get what they deserve. Fundamental attribution error (4.1) Blaming disposition, ignoring the situation. Both can lead to blaming victims; just-world adds the belief that life is fair.

items.k: What you need to be able to do
items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Would you give an obviously wrong answer just because everyone else did? Would you follow an order you thought was harmful? Would you help a stranger in trouble if a crowd was watching? Classic research says the situation matters far more than most of us like to admit. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Explain social norms, normative and informational influence, and the conditions that increase conformity and obedience. Explain persuasion: the central and peripheral routes, the halo effect, and the foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face techniques. How this shows up on the exam This topic is packed with terms that sound alike, so expect "which concept" questions. items.k: Social influence, conformity and obedience | Normative influence | Informational influence | Conformity and obedience | Conformity | Obedience | Social norms | Social influence theory | liked and accepted | know better | Ethics link
items.x: Social influence, conformity and obedience Social norms are the expectations and roles a society has for its members: how to behave in a classroom, at a wedding, in a queue. Social influence theory says pressure to think or act a certain way comes in two forms: Normative influence Going along with others to be liked and accepted , or to avoid rejection. Laughing at a joke you don't find funny because everyone else is laughing. Informational influence Going along with others because you believe they know better . In a new country, copying what locals do at a ceremony because you assume they know what is correct. Conformity and obedience Conformity Changing your behavior or beliefs to match a group's unspoken rules or expectations. In Solomon Asch's studies, many people gave obviously wrong answers about line lengths when everyone else in the room did. More likely when: the group is unanimous, the person feels insecure, the group is attractive or high-status, and responses are public. Obedience Complying with the directives of an authority figure. In Stanley Milgram's studies, most participants kept giving what they believed were painful shocks to another person when an experimenter told them to. More likely when: the authority is close by and seen as legitimate, the victim is distant, and no one else refuses. Ethics link Milgram's studies are often used to discuss research ethics: participants experienced serious stress and were deceived. Expect a question on which ethical guideline was a concern.

items.k: Persuasion | Central route | Peripheral route | Foot-in-the-door | Door-in-the-face | elaboration likelihood model | evidence and logical arguments | surface cues | halo effect | small request | large request
items.x: Persuasion Persuasion is the set of techniques used to convince yourself or others of an idea, action or belief. The elaboration likelihood model describes two routes: Central route Persuading with evidence and logical arguments . Works when people are motivated and able to think carefully, and tends to produce lasting change. A phone review comparing battery life, camera tests and price. Peripheral route Persuading with surface cues : attractiveness, celebrity, catchy music, emotion. Works when people are not thinking carefully; the change is often short-lived. A famous athlete smiling while holding the phone. The halo effect is a peripheral-route example: one positive trait (such as attractiveness) makes us assume a person has other positive traits too. Foot-in-the-door Start with a small request ; once someone agrees, a bigger one is more likely to be accepted. "Can I borrow a pen?" then "Can I borrow your notes for the week?" Door-in-the-face Start with a large request that will be refused, then make the smaller request you actually wanted. "Can you lend me 500 dirhams?" "No." "How about 50?"

items.k: Culture and groups | Superordinate goals | Social traps | Culture | Individualist | collectivist | Multiculturalism | Industrial-organizational (I/O) psychologists | burnout
items.x: Culture and groups Culture shapes how we see ourselves and others. Individualist cultures emphasize personal goals and independence; collectivist cultures emphasize group goals, family and interdependence. Multiculturalism , common in places like the UAE where many cultures live side by side, can broaden how people see themselves and others. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Effect What happens Trigger Example Group polarization Group discussion makes members' shared views more extreme. Discussing with like-minded people A group who slightly dislike a rule become strongly against it after talking. Groupthink The desire for harmony overrides realistic decision-making; doubts go unspoken. Pressure for agreement A project team approves a flawed plan because no one wants to argue. Diffusion of responsibility Each person feels less responsible when others are present. Shared responsibility Nobody reports a broken tap because everyone assumes someone else will. Social loafing People put in less effort when working as a group. Individual effort is hidden One member does most of the group presentation. Deindividuation Losing self-awareness and restraint in a group. Anonymity and arousal People post cruel comments online behind anonymous accounts. Social facilitation Performing better on simple or well-practiced tasks (and worse on hard ones) in front of others. An audience A skilled player performs better in the final with a crowd watching. False consensus effect Overestimating how much others agree with you. Assuming others think like you "Everyone thinks this homework is pointless." Superordinate goals Shared goals that require groups to cooperate. They reduce hostility and stereotyping between groups. Rival year groups working together to raise money for a charity. Social traps Situations where individuals act in their own self-interest, and everyone ends up worse off. Everyone uses the air conditioning at full power, and the building's system fails. Industrial-organizational (I/O) psychologists study how people perform at work: the best ways to manage work, how coworkers relate to one another, and how people feel about their jobs, including burnout (exhaustion and loss of motivation from long-term work stress).

items.k: Prosocial behavior | Altruism | Social reciprocity norm | Social responsibility norm | Bystander effect | social debt | Beat the bystander effect
items.x: Prosocial behavior Altruism Selfless concern for others and helping without expecting anything in return. Some researchers argue that people help partly because of social debt : a sense of obligation. Helping a stranger carry their bags with no reward. Social reciprocity norm The expectation that we should help those who have helped us. Helping a classmate revise because she helped you last month. Social responsibility norm The expectation that we should help those who depend on us or need help. Giving up your seat on the metro for an older passenger. Bystander effect People are less likely to help when others are present. Situational and attentional factors (how many people are there, whether they notice and interpret it as an emergency) predict helping. A person collapses in a busy mall, and everyone assumes someone else will act. Beat the bystander effect If you are the one who needs help in a crowd, point to one specific person: "You, in the blue shirt, call for help." That removes the diffusion of responsibility.

items.x: The psychodynamic view The psychodynamic theory, which grew out of Sigmund Freud's work, argues that unconscious processes drive personality: thoughts, wishes and memories we are not aware of still shape what we do. Freud described the mind as balancing three parts: the id (basic urges, wanting satisfaction now), the superego (our internalized sense of right and wrong) and the ego (the realistic part that tries to balance the two). Ego defense mechanisms When anxiety threatens the ego, it protects itself unconsciously with defense mechanisms. Test yourself: hide the names and identify each one from the example. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Defense mechanism What it does Example Denial Refusing to accept a painful reality. Insisting a failing grade must be a mistake, and not checking the work. Displacement Redirecting feelings toward a safer target. Being scolded by a teacher, then snapping at your younger brother at home. Projection Seeing your own unacceptable feelings in others. Someone who is jealous of a friend accuses the friend of being jealous of them. Rationalization Making up a logical-sounding excuse for behavior. "I didn't get into the team because the coach only picks his favorites." Reaction formation Acting the opposite of how you really feel. Being overly friendly to a classmate you actually dislike. Regression Returning to childlike behavior under stress. A teenager sulking and slamming doors like a young child after an argument. Repression Pushing painful memories or thoughts out of awareness. Having no memory of a frightening event from early childhood. Sublimation Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities. Turning anger into intense training at the gym. Assessing personality: projective tests Psychodynamic psychologists use projective tests , which present ambiguous material and ask people to interpret it, on the idea that their answers "project" preconscious and unconscious thoughts. Examples include inkblot tests and tests where people tell a story about an ambiguous picture. Critics point out that their scoring can be subjective, with weak reliability and validity (Topic 2.8).

items.x: The humanistic view Humanistic psychologists, such as Carl Rogers, focused on healthy growth and saw people as basically good, with a natural drive to fulfill their potential. Two ideas are central: Unconditional positive regard Accepting and valuing a person completely, without conditions, even when you disapprove of what they did. A parent who makes clear that their love doesn't depend on grades. Self-actualizing tendency The natural drive to grow and become the best version of yourself, which humanists saw as a primary motivation. Taking up a challenge simply because it helps you grow. Rogers argued that people raised with conditional regard ("I'll love you if you succeed") may learn to hide parts of themselves, while unconditional positive regard helps them grow.

Repression hides the memory; denial rejects the fact. Reaction formation Doing the opposite of what you feel. Sublimation Channeling an impulse into something acceptable. Reaction formation reverses the feeling; sublimation redirects its energy usefully. Rationalization A believable excuse. Regression Childlike behavior. One sounds reasonable; the other looks young.
