items.x: Trait theories and the Big Five Trait theories describe personality as a set of relatively stable characteristics that show up across situations. Instead of explaining why you are a certain way, they try to describe and measure how you are. The Big Five The best-supported trait model is the Big Five . Each trait is a spectrum: you can be anywhere from low to high. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Trait High scorers tend to be Low scorers tend to be Openness to experience Curious, creative, keen on new ideas and experiences. Practical, prefer routine and the familiar. Conscientiousness Organized, reliable, careful, self-disciplined. Spontaneous, disorganized, careless with deadlines. Extraversion Outgoing, talkative, energized by being with others. Reserved, quieter, energized by time alone. Agreeableness Kind, trusting, cooperative, helpful. Critical, competitive, suspicious of others. Emotional stability Calm, secure, steady under stress. Anxious, moody, easily upset. OCEAN Remember the Big Five as OCEAN : Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and N for Neuroticism . Neuroticism is simply the other end of emotional stability: high neuroticism means low emotional stability. Measuring traits Personality inventories Questionnaires where people rate how well statements describe them ("I am the life of the party"). They are scored objectively, which gives them better reliability than projective tests (4.4). Rating "I get my homework done on time" from 1 (not like me) to 5 (very like me). Factor analysis A statistical method that finds which test items cluster together, revealing the underlying traits. This is how researchers arrived at five broad factors. Answers about being talkative, sociable and outgoing all correlate, so they form one factor: extraversion.

items.x: Theories of motivation Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Theory Big idea Example Drive-reduction theory Biological needs create a drive (an unpleasant state of tension). We are motivated to reduce it and return to homeostasis , the body's balanced, steady state. You're thirsty after football practice, so you drink water. Arousal theory We are motivated to keep an optimal level of arousal : if we are under-stimulated we seek excitement, and if over-stimulated we seek calm. Bored at home, you go for a drive; after a hectic week, you want a quiet weekend. Self-determination theory We are motivated by needs for competence, connection and control. It distinguishes intrinsic motivation (doing something for its own sake) from extrinsic motivation (doing it for outside rewards or to avoid punishment). Drawing because you love it (intrinsic) versus drawing to win a prize (extrinsic). Incentive theory We are pulled toward behaviors by rewards (incentives) and pushed away by punishments. Working extra shifts to earn a bonus. Instinct theory Instincts are complex, unlearned behaviors shown by all members of a species. They are clear in non-human animals, but humans do not seem to show true instincts. Birds building nests or salmon swimming upstream to spawn. Push or pull? Drive reduction is a push from inside (a need). Incentive theory is a pull from outside (a reward). The Yerkes-Dodson law Linked to arousal theory, the Yerkes-Dodson law says performance is best at a moderate level of arousal. Too little and you're sluggish; too much and you panic. The best level depends on the task: easy or well-practiced tasks are performed best at higher arousal, while difficult or new tasks are performed best at lower arousal. Overjustification effect Paying people for something they already enjoy can reduce their intrinsic motivation. A child who loves reading may read less once you start paying them per book, because reading becomes "something I do for money".

items.x: Conflicts and sensation seeking Kurt Lewin described three kinds of motivational conflict : situations in which we have to choose between goals. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Conflict What it is Example Approach-approach Choosing between two attractive options. Two universities you love have both offered you a place. Approach-avoidance One option with both attractive and unattractive features. A job abroad pays well but means leaving your family. Avoidance-avoidance Choosing between two unattractive options. Staying up late to finish the essay or handing it in late. Sensation seeking Sensation seeking is the tendency to look for varied, new and intense experiences, and it differs from person to person. It has four parts: Experience seeking Looking for new sensations through the mind and senses. Traveling to unusual places, trying unfamiliar food. Thrill and adventure seeking Seeking physically exciting, risky activities. Skydiving, dune bashing, rock climbing. Disinhibition Seeking release through social activities and letting go of usual restraint. Being the loudest one at the party. Boredom susceptibility Strong dislike of repetition and routine. Getting restless when every day looks the same.

items.x: Eating and belongingness Hunger is a good example of how biology, environment and social life work together to motivate behavior. Ghrelin A hormone released by the empty stomach that signals hunger . Ghrelin "growls": it makes you want to eat. Leptin A hormone released by fat cells that signals fullness and reduces appetite. Leptin helps you "leave" the table. These signals are monitored by the hypothalamus , which helps regulate eating through its control of the pituitary gland and the hormones it triggers (Topic 1.3). External factors matter too: the presence of food (you eat more when a plate of dates is in front of you), the time of day (feeling hungry at lunchtime because it is lunchtime) and social gatherings (eating more at a family iftar or a wedding). Belongingness Humans also have a strong need to belong : to form and keep close relationships. Being included motivates a lot of behavior, from joining teams to keeping up with friends online, and being rejected or left out is painful and can lower motivation and well-being.

items.x: What emotion is and early theories An emotion (or affect ) is a subjective experience that involves physical arousal, expressive behavior and conscious thought, and it can shape how we think and act. Early theories disagreed about the order in which these parts happen. Picture yourself waiting backstage before a speech: 1. The body comes first Event → Body responds → Emotion felt 2. Body and feeling at the same time Event → Body responds Emotion felt 3. The body needs a label Event → Body responds → Cognitive label → Emotion felt Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Sequence What it claims Backstage example The body comes first The physical response happens first, and we feel the emotion when we notice it. "My heart is pounding, so I must be afraid." At the same time The physical response and the emotion happen together, independently. Your heart pounds and you feel afraid at the same moment. The body needs a label Arousal on its own is not enough; we need to interpret it with a cognitive label based on the situation. "My heart is pounding, and I'm about to give a speech, so this is nervousness." (At a football final, the same arousal might be labeled excitement.) Optional background These sequences match three classic theories: the body first (James-Lange), at the same time (Cannon-Bard) and the cognitive label (Schachter-Singer two-factor theory). items.x: Expressing emotion Facial-feedback hypothesis Our facial expressions can influence the emotions we feel, not just reveal them. Research results on this have been mixed . Holding a pen between your teeth (forcing a smile) may make cartoons seem slightly funnier. Broaden-and-build theory Positive emotions broaden our thinking and attention, which helps us build skills, relationships and resources over time. Feeling happy and relaxed, you try a new activity with friends and pick up a new skill. Emotion across cultures Paul Ekman's research suggested that six basic emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust) are expressed and recognized with similar facial expressions across cultures. However, findings on how universal these expressions are have been mixed , and culture clearly shapes emotion in two ways: Display rules Cultural norms about when, where and how strongly it is appropriate to show emotions. In some cultures, showing strong anger to an elder in public is seen as deeply disrespectful, so people hide it. Elicitors What triggers an emotion can differ across cultures and other groups, such as age and social class. A hand gesture that is friendly in one country may be offensive, and cause anger, in another. Living it In a multicultural school like ours, you have probably seen display rules in action: some classmates celebrate loudly and openly, while others show the same happiness with a quiet smile. Same emotion, different rules.

items.x: Stress and health Health psychology looks at how psychological, behavioral and social factors affect physical health, illness and wellness: why some people get sick more often, why people find it hard to change unhealthy habits, and how stress gets "under the skin". Stress and the body Stress makes us more susceptible to disorders and disease. It has been linked to hypertension (high blood pressure), headaches and immune suppression , which is why you are more likely to catch that cold during a stressful week. Eustress Stress we see as motivating : a challenge that energizes us. The nervous excitement before a football final that helps you focus. Distress Stress we see as debilitating : it overwhelms us and wears us down. Feeling paralyzed by a pile of deadlines you can't see a way through. Traumatic stress Stress from a major, often sudden, threatening event. Being in a serious car accident. Daily hassles Small, everyday irritations that build up over time. Traffic every morning, a phone that keeps dying, a noisy neighbor. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are stressful or traumatic experiences in childhood, such as neglect, losing a parent or living with serious conflict at home. They are sources of stress that can affect a person throughout the lifespan, raising the risk of health and psychological problems in adulthood.

items.x: How we react to stress Hans Selye described the general adaptation syndrome (GAS) : the process the body goes through when it faces stress. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Phase What happens Example: a two-week exam period Alarm reaction The stressor is first encountered and the body reacts with a fight, flight or freeze response. Resistance briefly dips. The timetable comes out and your heart races. Resistance The body confronts the stressor, staying highly aroused to cope. You keep going on late nights and adrenaline through the first week. Exhaustion The stress subsides or the body's resources are spent. This is when we are most susceptible to illness . The day after the last exam, you come down with a fever. Tend and befriend Not everyone fights or flees. The tend-and-befriend theory proposes that some people react to stress by caring for their own needs and the needs of others, and by seeking connection with others. Research suggests this response is seen more often in women. Example: after hearing of a family emergency, someone gathers relatives together, makes food for everyone and keeps checking in on each person.

items.k: Coping with stress | Problem-focused coping | Emotion-focused coping | problem to solve | emotional reaction | Which works better
items.x: Coping with stress Problem-focused coping Seeing the stress as a problem to solve , and working on solutions until one works. Stressed about a group project, you make a schedule, divide the tasks and message the teacher with a question. Emotion-focused coping Managing your emotional reaction to the stress, rather than the stressor itself. Strategies include deep breathing, meditation, or medication aimed at reducing stressful emotions. The night before the exam, you do some deep breathing and go for a walk to calm down. Which works better? It depends on whether the situation can be changed. Problem-focused coping helps when you have control (studying for a test). Emotion-focused coping helps when you don't (waiting for exam results).

Exhaustion phase Resources spent; illness most likely. If the person has just got sick after a long stressful stretch, it's exhaustion. Problem-focused coping Changing the situation. Emotion-focused coping Changing how you feel about it. Ask: is the person tackling the cause, or calming the feeling? Traumatic stress A major, threatening event. Daily hassles Small irritations that add up. Size and frequency: one big event, or many small ones.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do For most of its history, psychology focused on what goes wrong: disorders, damage, dysfunction. Positive psychology asks the opposite question. What helps people do well? What makes a life go right? It's a short topic, but it connects to almost everything in this unit. items.x: What helps people thrive Positive psychology seeks to identify the factors that lead to well-being, resilience, positive emotions and psychological health . Subjective well-being is how satisfied and happy people say they are with their lives. Positive subjective experiences Gratitude Expressing gratitude increases subjective well-being . Writing down three things you're thankful for each night, or messaging a teacher to thank them. Signature strengths People who regularly use their signature strengths (their own best character strengths) report more happiness and higher subjective well-being. A naturally kind student who volunteers to help new students settle in. Six categories of virtues Researchers built a classification of character strengths around six categories of virtues : Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Virtue What it covers Example strengths Wisdom Strengths of knowing and thinking. Curiosity, creativity, love of learning. Courage Strengths of acting despite fear or difficulty. Bravery, persistence, honesty. Humanity Strengths of caring for others. Kindness, love, social intelligence. Justice Strengths of fairness and community. Fairness, teamwork, leadership. Temperance Strengths of self-control and moderation. Forgiveness, humility, self-regulation. Transcendence Strengths that connect us to something larger and give meaning. Gratitude, hope, appreciation of beauty. Remember the six W ise C ourageous H umans J ustly T emper T roubles: Wisdom, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, Transcendence.

items.x: Resilience and posttraumatic growth Resilience The ability to cope with and recover from difficulty. A student who fails a test, figures out what went wrong and bounces back. Posttraumatic growth Positive psychological change that can come after trauma or serious stress: new appreciation for life, stronger relationships, a clearer sense of purpose. After surviving a serious illness, someone says they now value their family more and have found a new direction in life. Growth is not the absence of pain Posttraumatic growth doesn't mean the trauma was good or that the person no longer struggles. It means that positive change can happen alongside the difficulty.

Humanity Caring for individuals: kindness, love. Justice Fairness in groups: teamwork, leadership. One-to-one care versus fairness to the community. Temperance Self-control and moderation. Transcendence Meaning, hope, gratitude. Temperance holds you back from excess; transcendence connects you to something larger.

items.x: Start here What you need to be able to do Everyone feels anxious, sad or a bit odd sometimes. So where is the line between a difficult day and a psychological disorder? This topic is about how psychologists draw that line, what labels can do for (and to) people, and how each perspective you met in Unit 0 explains what causes a disorder. By the end of this page, you should be able to: Describe how dysfunction, distress and deviation from social norms are used to identify psychological disorders. Explain the positive and negative consequences of diagnosis. Describe the DSM and the ICD, and why diagnosis needs specialized training. Explain how each psychological perspective explains disorders, and why most psychologists take an eclectic approach. Explain the biopsychosocial model and the diathesis-stress model. A note before you start This topic is about understanding, not diagnosing. Many symptoms on this page are things everyone experiences sometimes; a disorder is about how intense, lasting and disruptive they are, and only a trained professional can decide that. If anything here feels close to home, please talk to the school counselor or an adult you trust. How this shows up on the exam Expect a scenario asking which perspective a psychologist is taking when explaining a disorder, or asking you to apply the diathesis-stress model. Remember: no single criterion (such as being unusual) is enough on its own to define a disorder.

items.x: Defining and diagnosing disorders Psychologists consider several factors together when deciding whether behavior is a psychological disorder: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Factor The question it asks Example Dysfunction Does it get in the way of everyday life: school, work, relationships, self-care? Anxiety so strong that a student can no longer attend classes. Distress Does the person experience it as upsetting or painful? Constant worry that leaves someone exhausted and unhappy. Deviation from social norms Is it very different from what is typical or expected in that culture? Hearing voices that no one else hears. Unusual is not the same as disordered Deviation alone isn't enough: being a chess prodigy is unusual, but not a disorder. Norms also differ across cultures and change over time, which is why the context matters. The double edge of diagnosis Positive consequences A diagnosis can give access to effective treatment and support, help people understand what they're experiencing, and help professionals communicate and research. A student finally diagnosed with ADHD gets extra exam time and learns strategies that help. Negative consequences Labels can bring stigma and discrimination, change how others treat the person, and shape how people see themselves. Cultural and societal norms, racism, ageism and other biases can also affect who gets diagnosed and how. Classmates start treating someone differently once they hear about a diagnosis. Classification systems Diagnosing a disorder requires specialized training and the use of evidence-based diagnostic tools . Two major classification systems are used, and both are updated regularly as research and practice advance: DSM The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders , developed by the American Psychiatric Association . Widely used by clinicians in the United States. ICD The International Classification of Diseases , developed by the World Health Organization . Used around the world, including for health records.

items.x: Explaining the causes of disorders Each perspective from Unit 0 points to a different kind of cause. Imagine explaining why someone has a strong fear of driving: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Perspective Causes of disorders focus on... Fear of driving Behavioral Maladaptive learned associations between stimuli and responses. A minor crash was paired with terror, and the fear became conditioned to cars. Psychodynamic Unconscious thoughts and experiences, often from childhood. A buried childhood conflict is being expressed as fear. Humanistic A lack of social support and being unable to fulfill one's potential. Feeling unsupported and stuck, the person's fears have taken over. Cognitive Maladaptive thoughts, beliefs, attitudes or emotions . "If I drive, I will definitely crash." Evolutionary Behaviors and mental processes that reduce the likelihood of survival . A useful alertness to danger has become so extreme that it now gets in the way of normal life. Sociocultural Maladaptive social and cultural relationships and dynamics. Family members constantly talk about how dangerous the roads are. Biological Physiological or genetic issues. An overactive amygdala, or a family history of anxiety. In practice, most psychologists use an eclectic approach : they draw on more than one perspective when diagnosing and treating clients. Interaction models Biopsychosocial model Any psychological problem may involve a combination of biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Depression linked to genes (bio), negative thinking (psych) and social isolation (social). Diathesis-stress model Disorders develop when a genetic vulnerability (the diathesis) combines with stressful life experiences (the stress). Someone with a family history of depression develops it only after losing their job. Their sibling, with the same genes but less stress, doesn't. Think of a match The diathesis is the match; the stress is the strike. A match on its own doesn't light, and striking nothing doesn't make fire. You need both.

items.x: Neurodevelopmental disorders Neurodevelopmental disorders begin during the developmental period (childhood). Symptoms are judged by whether a person's behavior is appropriate for their age or maturity. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) A persistent pattern of inattention (difficulty staying focused, losing things, being easily distracted) and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity (fidgeting, interrupting, acting without thinking), beyond what is typical for the person's age. A student who can't stay seated, constantly loses homework and blurts out answers, at a level that disrupts school and home life. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) Ongoing differences in social communication and interaction , along with restricted, repetitive behaviors or interests. It's a spectrum: support needs range widely from person to person. A child who finds back-and-forth conversation hard, follows the same routines every day and knows everything about train timetables. Possible causes: environmental, physiological or genetic.

items.x: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders Schizophrenia spectrum disorders involve problems in one or more of five areas. Schizophrenia can be acute (sudden, often in response to stress) or chronic (long-lasting). Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Symptom Positive or negative? What it looks like Delusions Positive False beliefs , such as delusions of persecution ("Everyone is plotting against me") or grandeur ("I have special powers"). Hallucinations Positive False perceptions in any sense, most often hearing voices. Disorganized thinking or speech Positive Jumping between unrelated ideas, or word salad : words strung together in nonsensical ways. Disorganized motor behavior (catatonia) Positive or negative Catatonic excitement (a positive symptom: agitated, purposeless movement) or catatonic stupor (a negative symptom: little or no movement). Negative symptoms Negative The absence of typical behavior, such as flat affect (little emotional expression) or lack of movement. Positive and negative are not good and bad Think math, not mood. Positive symptoms are added to typical experience (voices, false beliefs). Negative symptoms are typical behaviors that have been taken away (emotion, movement, speech). Possible causes: a genetic or biological link, such as prenatal exposure to a virus , or imbalances in certain neurotransmitters. The dopamine hypothesis proposes that too much dopamine activity contributes to positive symptoms.

items.x: Depressive and bipolar disorders Depressive disorders involve a sad, empty or irritable mood along with physical and cognitive changes (in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration) that affect a person's ability to function. Major depressive disorder Episodes of at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest in almost everything, with other symptoms such as changes in sleep and energy, feelings of worthlessness and difficulty concentrating. Someone who has lost all interest in activities they used to love, sleeps most of the day and feels worthless. Persistent depressive disorder A milder but long-lasting depressed mood, present most days for at least two years. Someone who has felt low and flat most days for years, though still gets through work and school. Bipolar disorders involve periods of mania (abnormally elevated mood and energy, little need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky decisions) and periods of depression . Bipolar cycling is moving between these states, and each period can last different amounts of time. Bipolar I disorder At least one episode of full mania , severe enough to seriously disrupt life (episodes of depression are common too). Someone who stays awake for days, spends their savings and believes they will soon be world-famous. Bipolar II disorder Episodes of hypomania (a milder form of mania) and episodes of major depression . Someone who goes through weeks of deep depression, then a few days of unusual energy and productivity. Possible causes of depressive and bipolar disorders: biological, genetic, social, cultural, behavioral or cognitive sources.

items.x: Anxiety disorders Anxiety disorders involve excessive fear or anxiety with related changes in behavior. Test yourself: hide the disorder names and identify each one. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Disorder Key feature Example Specific phobia Intense fear of a specific object or situation , such as acrophobia (heights) or arachnophobia (spiders). Refusing to visit the observation deck of a tall tower because of fear of heights. Agoraphobia Intense fear of situations where escape might be hard: public transportation, open spaces, enclosed spaces like shops and cinemas, queues or crowds, or being outside the home alone. Avoiding the metro and malls, and eventually not leaving home at all. Panic disorder Repeated, unexpected panic attacks : sudden, overwhelming waves of fear with physical symptoms like a racing heart and difficulty breathing. Suddenly feeling as though you're having a heart attack while sitting quietly in class. Social anxiety disorder Intense fear of being judged or watched by others. Avoiding speaking in class or eating in front of others for fear of embarrassment. Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) Prolonged, nonspecific anxiety and worry about many things. Constantly worrying about grades, health, family and money, without a clear trigger. Culture-bound forms Ataque de nervios A culture-bound form of panic , experienced mainly by people of Caribbean or Iberian descent. Sudden episodes of uncontrollable shouting, crying and trembling, often after a family stressor. Taijin kyofusho A culture-bound form of social anxiety , experienced mainly by Japanese people, involving fear that others judge one's body as undesirable or offensive. Fear that one's appearance or body might offend others. Possible causes: learned associations between stimuli (conditioning), maladaptive thinking or emotional responses, and biological or genetic sources.

items.x: OCD, dissociative disorders and PTSD Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders These involve obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors done to address the obsessions). Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) Obsessions and compulsions that take up a lot of time and cause distress. An intrusive fear of germs (obsession) leads to washing hands until they crack (compulsion). Hoarding disorder Persistent difficulty throwing things away, whatever their value, leading to cluttered living spaces. Rooms so full of old newspapers and bags that they can no longer be used. Possible causes: learned associations, maladaptive thinking or emotional responses, and biological or genetic sources. Dissociative disorders These involve dissociation : a disconnection in consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control or behavior. Dissociative amnesia Being unable to recall important personal information, usually linked to trauma or stress. With fugue , the person also travels away or wanders, confused about their identity. After a traumatic event, someone can't remember a whole period of their life; with fugue, they turn up in another city unsure how they got there. Dissociative identity disorder (DID) Two or more distinct identities or personality states, with gaps in memory. A person who discovers notes in their own handwriting that they don't remember writing, in a style unlike their own. Possible causes: the experience of trauma or stress. Trauma and stressor-related disorders Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) follows exposure to a traumatic or stressful event, with lasting psychological distress. Symptoms may include hypervigilance (always on alert), severe anxiety, flashbacks , insomnia, emotional detachment and hostility. Example: someone who survived a building fire jumps at every alarm, has flashbacks of the smoke and can't sleep. Possible causes: the experience of trauma or stress.

items.x: Eating and personality disorders Feeding and eating disorders These involve changes in eating or the absorption of food that harm a person's health or psychological functioning. Anorexia nervosa Restricting food intake to a dangerous degree, alongside an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted view of one's own body. The key feature is serious restriction and a distorted body image. Bulimia nervosa Repeated episodes of binge eating followed by behaviors to compensate for it, such as purging. The key feature is the cycle of binging and compensating. Possible causes: biological, genetic, social, cultural, behavioral or cognitive sources. Support Eating disorders are serious health conditions, and they are treatable. If you're worried about yourself or a friend, please speak to the school counselor or the school nurse. Personality disorders Personality disorders are enduring patterns of inner experience and behavior that differ markedly from the person's culture, are pervasive and inflexible , begin in adolescence or early adulthood , are stable over time , and lead to distress or impairment. Cluster B Dramatic, emotional or erratic Antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic and borderline personality disorders. items.x: Research, trends and ethics Researchers who have run meta-analyses (studies that combine the results of many studies) of psychotherapy conclude that psychotherapies are generally effective . Many psychologists use evidence-based interventions : treatments supported by research. Therapeutic alliance A relationship of trust and shared goals between therapist and client. It is one of the strongest predictors of successful therapy. A client feels genuinely heard and works with the therapist on goals they agreed together. Cultural humility A therapist's openness to learning about, and respecting, the client's culture, rather than assuming their own view is the norm. A therapist asks how the client's family and faith shape the way they see their difficulties. From asylums to communities As psychotropic medications became more widely used and more effective, hospitals and asylums deinstitutionalized huge numbers of people in the late 20th century. Today, treatment is decentralized (in communities and clinics rather than large institutions), often combining medication with psychological therapy . Ethical principles Psychologists in clinical settings must follow ethical principles set by the APA, including: Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Principle What it means Nonmaleficence Do no harm. Fidelity Be trustworthy and faithful to your responsibilities to clients. Integrity Be honest, accurate and truthful. Respect for people's rights and dignity Respect clients' privacy, confidentiality and right to make their own decisions.

items.x: Psychological therapies Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Approach Goal Key techniques Psychodynamic Uncover the unconscious mind and bring hidden conflicts into awareness. Free association (saying whatever comes to mind) and dream interpretation . Cognitive Change maladaptive thinking . Cognitive restructuring (identifying and challenging distorted thoughts) and fear hierarchies . Focuses on the cognitive triad . Behavioral (applied behavior analysis) Use the principles of conditioning to change behavior. Exposure therapies such as systematic desensitization , aversion therapy , token economies and biofeedback . Cognitive-behavioral (CBT) Combine cognitive and behavioral techniques. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT) . Humanistic (person-centered) Help the client grow in a supportive, accepting relationship. Active listening and unconditional positive regard . The cognitive triad Cognitive therapy proposes that people with depression tend to hold negative thoughts about three things : themselves, the world and the future. Therapy targets all three. Behavioral techniques up close Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Technique How it works Example Systematic desensitization Gradual exposure to a fear, step by step up a fear hierarchy, while staying relaxed. Relaxation replaces fear (counterconditioning). Someone afraid of flying first looks at photos of planes, then visits an airport, then sits in a plane on the ground. Aversion therapy Pairing an unwanted behavior with something unpleasant, so the behavior becomes linked with discomfort. Painting bitter-tasting polish on nails to stop nail biting. Token economy Earning tokens for desired behaviors that can be exchanged for rewards (operant conditioning). In a residential program, patients earn points for making their beds and attending sessions, then trade them for privileges. Biofeedback Using monitors to show body signals (heart rate, muscle tension) so the person learns to control them, helping regulate the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. Watching a heart rate monitor while practicing slow breathing to calm anxiety. Group and individual therapy In individual therapy , one client works one-to-one with a therapist, with full attention and privacy. In group therapy , a therapist works with several clients at once. Group therapy costs less per person, shows people that others share their problems, and lets members give and receive support and feedback. Family therapy treats the family as a system, and self-help or support groups bring together people facing the same challenge. Hypnosis Hypnosis has been shown to be effective in treating pain and anxiety . Research does not support using it to retrieve accurate memories or to "regress" people to an earlier age: hypnotized people can confidently "remember" things that never happened.

items.x: Biological treatments Biological treatments target possible biochemical or physical causes of disorders. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Treatment What it is Used for Antidepressants Medications that interact with neurotransmitters such as serotonin. Depression, and often anxiety. Antianxiety drugs Medications that reduce feelings of anxiety and tension. Anxiety disorders. Lithium A mood-stabilizing medication. Bipolar disorders. Antipsychotics Medications that reduce dopamine activity. Schizophrenia (especially positive symptoms). Psychoactive medications can have side effects . For example, long-term use of some antipsychotics can cause tardive dyskinesia , a movement disorder (involuntary movements, often of the face and tongue) related to the regulation of dopamine. Test yourself: hide the answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Intervention What it involves Psychosurgery Surgery that removes or destroys (lesions) brain tissue to change behavior. The lobotomy was popular in the mid-20th century but is rarely, if ever, performed today. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) Magnetic pulses from a coil held near the scalp stimulate brain activity; it is noninvasive. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) A brief electric current is passed through the brain under anesthesia, causing a short seizure. Used mainly for severe depression that hasn't responded to other treatments.

Cognitive therapy Change the thoughts. Behavioral therapy Change the behavior through conditioning. CBT combines both. Psychodynamic therapy Uncover the unconscious; the therapist interprets. Person-centered therapy Active listening; the client leads. Who's in charge of the meaning: the analyst or the client? TMS Magnetic pulses; no seizure.
